The framework I am building does not push content out of the picture. Instead, it shifts the center of gravity. Rather than organizing everything around what students should know at each step, it organizes opportunities around how students learn, revise, and take ownership of their thinking across whatever content they encounter. Content still matters, but it is no longer the anchor. The anchor is cognescience itself.

Accepting curriculum as contexture may do something unexpected for the field. It may allow curriculum theory to become more unified, more accepted, less easily dismissed or pushed to the margins of educational discourse. If curriculum is understood as inherently relational, then the fragmentation that has long plagued the field stops looking like dysfunction and starts looking like honesty. Different perspectives are not competing for the one true definition; they are each describing the concept from the vantage point available to them.

At the same time, at the level of the individual learner, contexture does fragment. It fragments goals, duties, responsibilities. It does not hand students a single destination and a single route. It removes certain constraints and replaces them with freedom, with wander, with endospective exploration. But here is the strange part: by allowing that fragmentation, by building it into the design rather than treating it as deviation, the fracturing stops feeling fractured. When exploration is the expectation rather than the exception, there is nothing to fragment against. The learner is not being pulled away from some "real" path. The path is the exploration itself.

This only looks like chaos from the outside. To an AP student whose assigned goal is passing a single test at the end of the year, of course the opportunities of exploration seem like distractions from the thing that actually matters. But that is only because the content-anchored system has already told that student what matters. Remove that prior assignment, and the fragmentation dissolves. All is one and one is all.
This is the definition of curriculum I am working with. It is not a universal definition, and it is not a rejection of other definitions. It is a reorientation.

If curriculum is relational, shaped by the positions and purposes of whoever is thinking about it, then the concept itself cannot be separated from the people who use it. The previous section argued that the fragmentation of curriculum theory is not a failure but a clue. Different perspectives are not competing for the one true definition; they are each describing the concept from the vantage point available to them. Accepting this means accepting that curriculum, understood as contexture, does not exist apart from its interpreters. It is not a thing waiting to be discovered. It is a space that forms and reforms depending on who enters it, what they bring, and what they are trying to do. The anchor is no longer content. The anchor is cognescience. But even that reorientation leaves something unresolved.

If curriculum bends depending on where you stand, then the next question becomes unavoidable: whose positions have historically won? The earlier sections of this paper traced how content became the fixed anchor of American schooling, how frameworks were layered on top without ever questioning the foundation, and how sequences and assessments reinforced a logic of coverage and compliance. That logic did not appear from nowhere. It was built by people, defended by institutions, and maintained by systems that benefited from keeping it in place. Reframing curriculum as contexture does not automatically undo those histories. It does not erase the structures that decide which reforms are allowed to scale and which are quietly dismissed. A relational concept is still dominated by certain relations.

This brings us to the question of power. If curriculum is shaped by context, then who shapes the context? If change is possible, then who gets to define what counts as change? The sections that follow examine how curriculum has been influenced, directed, and constrained by forces far beyond the classroom. Theorists respond to their eras; society absorbs and distorts their ideas; conservative and progressive movements push and pull against each other for control of what schooling is allowed to become. Understanding who moves curriculum is essential before proposing how to move it differently.

By this point, we’ve spent a lot of time on what curriculum is not. It is not just a list of content standards, not just a scope and sequence, not just a set of assessments that pretend to measure everything that matters. I’ve argued that American public schools have often treated content as the fixed anchor while frameworks, sequences, and tests orbit around it. If the purpose of schooling is shifting from what to learn toward how to learn, then that anchor starts to look less secure. The next question, then, is not “Which content should we prioritize?” but “What do we even mean by curriculum if we take how students learn seriously?”

This question has never had a neat answer. In grad school, I was in a Foundations of Curriculum graduate course that was partially organized around six different ways of orienting theoretical constructions of curriculum: curriculum as Product, Process, Practice, Praxis, Political, and Personal. We studied “curriculum” as something slightly different each week: a technical plan with objectives and outcomes, a set of interactions between teachers and learners, a vehicle for justice, a form of reflective action, a political project about whose knowledge counts, and an autobiographical journey. We didn’t resolve the question “What is curriculum?” so much as multiply it.

My goal in this chapter is not to add one more official definition to the pile. I’m less interested in declaring what curriculum is in a universal sense than in paying attention to what different people seem to be trying to do when they use the word. The sheer number of “curriculum as…” options suggests that curriculum may not be a single object waiting to be named, but a set of decisions about what learning should be and how it should unfold. In the next section, I look more closely at that apparent fragmentation, not as a failure to be fixed, but as a clue to what is really at stake when we talk about curriculum at all.

children.title: WHO
children.spine: Power flows through curriculum — who designs it, who enforces it, and who is excluded by it.

children.title: WHO IS IN CHARGE? WHO ENACTS CHANGE? WHO HAS THE POWER?

paragraphs.text: Dewey was a product of the progressive era. His career began at a time of industrialization, the beginning of automation, and a multitude of reform. This era saw change across all fields. American historians of the era transitioned their framing of the early republic to call out the greed and selfishness of the Founding Fathers – the first of this type of rhetoric from prominent historians. Women’s suffrage was sprawling with determined female fighters leading to one of the four amendments to the Constitution in less than a decade. Jazz music introduced a blend and ownership of art and expression by a suppressed group of people during the Harlem Renaissance. This was indeed a progressive era of change and reformation.

Unfortunately for Dewey, his influence didn’t come early enough; adaptation was thrust on Americans. Corruption overpowered success, and in a dust storm of bad timing, the gold plating of the US economy washed away. After the tumult of the Great Depression and the Second World War, nationalism began to shroud the complexities and nuances of curriculum. Very steadily over the next few decades, the liberal humanists reclaimed the prominence of accessible curriculum, but the economic backdrop had fundamentally changed. The industrial economy that birthed Dewey was dying, giving way after World War II to the Corporate Age. In this new era of managerial hierarchies and specialized roles, the messy, organic community Dewey envisioned was increasingly viewed as insufficient. The educational landscape shifted from a focus on the child’s natural "growth" to a demand for measurable results and systemic efficiency.

The Corporate Era is a very interesting narrative of US history largely unexplored by traditional historians. When the US government began breaking out the robber barons’ monopolies, the Rockefellers knew their strategy had to switch. A monopoly controls only one sector, but public education has the power to control knowledge. John D. Rockefeller’s son, also named John, created the General Education Board, one that provided more funding for US public education than the entire federal government for decades following WWI. The university where Dewey studied, the university where he taught, and the Lincoln School that assumed Dewey’s philosophies were all funded by the Rockefeller’s Board.

After WWI, corruption became fueled not by outright takeovers, but by subtle complex deals. This new era required a new architectural logic, which arrived in 1949 with Ralph Tyler. Tyler didn't just offer a philosophy; he offered a "rationale" – a word he uses repeatedly to describe a "systematic attack" on the problems of curriculum making. Tyler argued that because contemporary life is "so complex" and "continually changing," educators could no longer afford to "waste the time of students" on learning things that were no longer significant. The intuitive, ‘hit-or-miss judgment’ of the past was no longer.

Tyler represents the perfect case study of the reciprocal "give-and-take" relationship between theorist and society. His intent was to create a balanced, pragmatic framework where objectives weren't just guessed at, but derived from three distinct sources: "Studies of the Learners Themselves," "Studies of Contemporary Life," and "Suggestions About Objectives from Subject Specialists.” He explicitly warned that "no single source of information is adequate" to provide a basis for wise decisions, even arguing that a "comprehensive philosophy of education" was necessary to screen these objectives, ensuring they weren't just contradictory lists of facts (Tyler, 1949, pp. 4, 5).

However, the mainstream curriculum (echoing the accelerating corporate obsession with efficiency) did something else. The GEB provided the funding for Tyler to publish his research but only adopted his objective-first framework while ignoring his insistence on philosophical balance. Schools had no choice but to co-opt his tool or lose funding due to legislation lobbied by the GEB. This now meant that no school would receive funding without filling in the 'objectives' primarily with the views of "Subject Specialists," which Tyler himself noted was already the "source of objectives most commonly used in typical schools" (Tyler, 1949, p. 25).

This demonstrates how a theorist (Tyler) offered a holistic rationale, but society (the new Corporate structure) took his mechanical framework and gave it a different purpose, bending the theory to fit a need for standardization. It also demonstrates again how a theorist was influenced by his place in time. Tyler did not invent the obsession with efficiency but merely codified it, responding to a society that had "laid upon the schools" a burden of "tremendous increase in knowledge" that could no longer be managed by the "older and slower" traditions of the past (Tyler, 1949, pp. 16–17). Whether intentional or not, designing assessments around the primarily set objectives mimics an optimized, efficient workstream.
The "Tyler Rationale" became a synonym for rigid objective-setting, proving that curriculum, theorists, and society are in a constant, reciprocal, and often distorting relationship.

The Corporate Era reinforced a societal norm of efficiency, clarity, and optimization. Because of this, measurement was more structured and consistent. Job requirements remained as narrow as they were in the Industrial Era, and measurements of skill were told to you in the form of a pay check. The 60’s introduced another score of counterculture movement, similar to that of the progressive era a half century before. For the first time in US society, students themselves became drivers of societal change. The landmark Brown v. Board of Education case was not spearheaded by someone out of school, nor was it spearheaded by a political leader – it was spearheaded because of an actual student.

This student and her family, with the help and support of the ACLU, eventually led to the President sending his national guard to Arkansas to escort the student to school safely. This fits into a much broader theme of the counterculture movement. The ideas of race were shifting. Fear of equality and change fueled debates and protests throughout politics, society, and education.

Action took place at higher levels of education as well. A number of colleges began to speak out against their country, something that would have disrupted the entirety of Harvard, Yale, or William and Mary decades ago. Activists spoke out against race, gender, and sexuality inequality, the Vietnam War, and the very identity of the United States. The GEB dissolved and David Rockefeller founded the Trilateral Commission, instituting globalist priorities. Tension between Social Meliorists and Liberal Humanists rose and vied for dominance, polarizing parts of the nation.

Why was this happening? Because a sense of uniformity was emerging. A sense of right and wrong, fair and unfair, important and unimportant. This right and wrong made it easier to spot differences and discrepancies; it trained you to look for what’s different from each other rather than what’s similar. For instance, was it fair that a woman who did the exact same job as a man get rewarded for her success less? Does that mean she is inferior? We can watch the work they complete, they measured the same, but are rewarded differently. The ideals of corporate America swept through society. Measuring a person’s worth against another became easier than ever. And schools reflected this.

Curriculum dominance began to fracture. No longer did one philosophy control the way schools functioned. Ironically, as curriculum shifts away from the glorification and nationalism of US history, curriculum itself is more politically swayed than Jefferson, Mann, or Dewey would have suggested. This push and pull relationship between many powerful branches make this a difficult analysis. Should teachers be forced to align their lessons with that based in their course textbook? Should a single company be allowed to design textbooks for more than half of all students? Should those same textbook companies receive funding from global corporations?

When examining how change in curriculum is influenced, the answer does not lie in a specific “who” or “what.” Rather, a symbiotic network of philosophies and ideologies push and pull at each other pressuring change or resistance by those in different circumstances. When it comes down to it, everyone indirectly affects change in curriculum by the influence they have on others; yet ones influence is limited by their experience. I will attempt to demonstrate this push and pull nature of society, educators, theorists, and students by presenting the documented philosophies with the greatest influence on change in the current day.

children.title: “Educating the Right Way” – tool of change

paragraphs.text: If Tyler reveals the mechanisms through which curriculum responds to pressure from society, the profession, and local practice, Michael Apple pushes further: who governs those "common sense" mechanisms, and whose interests do they serve? For Apple, curriculum is never a neutral list of facts. It is a political project that selects some knowledge as normal, hides other knowledge as marginal, and then treats those choices as common sense. The question underneath his entire analysis is the same one driving this chapter: not just what is taught, but who has the power to define what teaching is for.

Apple argues that in our current moment, that power is largely in conservative hands. He calls the dominant project “conservative modernization” and shows how it knots together four anchors – markets, standards, God, and inequality – into a single common sense about schooling. These anchors don’t just describe the system, they steer it. When markets become the natural language of education, reform only sounds legitimate if it promises choice, efficiency, or “return on investment.” When standards and test scores are treated as the only serious evidence, any proposal that cannot be translated into measurable outcomes is quietly dismissed. When religious nationalism and “traditional values” are framed as the moral center, questions about race, gender, or power are easily recast as distractions from the “basics.” Inequality, in this arrangement, does not appear as something designed; it shows up as the predictable result of individual effort in a competitive system (Apple, 2005).

The important point for my argument is not that conservatives have strong opinions, that has always been true, but that they sit at the choke points of change. Apple’s coalition of neoliberals, neoconservatives, authoritarian populists, and managerial professionals may disagree on details, but together they control the levers that decide which reforms can scale: state standards, textbook adoptions, testing regimes, teacher evaluation systems, accountability policies (Apple, 2005). They design the metrics, write the rules, and manage the data dashboards that define what “improvement” even means. In Apple’s words, they have “engaged in a vast social and ideological project” to redefine the basic categories of schooling: what counts as achievement, what counts as responsibility, what counts as democracy. Once those categories are in place, whole swaths of critical or justice-oriented work can be ruled out without ever being debated.

Amplification is the main tool used by those with power. What Apple’s analysis lacked was a structured understanding of elitist membership networks in fields controlling knowledge. In his defense, you won’t easily find an answer examining who has the power to define what teaching is for. Corporations placing members in positions of power and influence is the clearest example of direct macro level change in shaping what teaching is for. The traditional content-first approach can benefit anyone with the power to define what constitutes ‘legitimate’ content. Because curriculum is so fragmented, a modern monopoly over knowledge constitutes many nodes working together.

The content-first approach is only a means to an end, the end being a continuation of a corporate economy where wealth is determined by meeting someone else’s objectives. The end itself is a means, a means to stay in control, a means to stay in power. Amplification of aligned knowledge, rather than suppressing opposing forms of knowledge, is a much more optimized process. Dewey was the most respected name in the field when the GEB took his name, but not his work – even though Dewey worked as a professor down the hall from the newly designed Lincoln school. Ralph Tyler designed the architecture for the cycle, so the GEB lobbied for legislation using his name. Pinar and Freire spoke out against the system and weren’t silenced; they just remained in college lecture halls and not in K-12 instruction.

Seen this way, the right does not simply block change; it organizes it. Conservative modernization uses schools as a tool to reshape common sense and identity, not just policy. As Apple notes, one of its core accomplishments is to “alter the meanings of the most basic categories” we use to understand ourselves. “Good schooling” becomes synonymous with high scores on standardized measures of narrow content. “Democracy” is emptied of its political struggle and remade as an economic concept organized around competition and choice. The result is a system where even progressive-sounding reforms are often forced to justify themselves in conservative terms: raising test scores, increasing workforce readiness, closing “achievement gaps” so students can compete more effectively in the same unequal market.

His point is not just that conservatives have won some policy battles. It is that they currently control the language and infrastructure through which large-scale educational change is allowed to travel. If you want a new curriculum to move beyond one classroom or one school, you almost always have to route it through their anchors -  markets, standards, God, and the existing distribution of inequality. You design your unit so it “aligns to state standards.” You frame your culturally responsive lessons as ways to boost reading scores. You argue that anti-racist work will make students more employable in a diverse economy. In doing so, you use conservative modernization as a tool, even when you are trying to push against its purposes.

If conservative forces currently shape the terms of acceptable change, then progressive educators are left with a constrained set of choices. They can ignore the dominant system and work only in local, often fragile pockets. They can try to bend conservative tools toward more just ends, speaking the language of markets and standards while smuggling in different purposes. Or they can attempt to build forms of change that refuse those anchors altogether -  an option that Apple suggests is necessary but far from easy, given how deeply conservative modernization has seeped into our shared common sense.

The next section takes up that problem directly. If the right uses schools as a top-down tool for directing collective change, what kinds of change are left (literally and politically) for projects like culturally relevant education, culturally responsive pedagogy, and anti-racist curricula? How do those approaches operate when they are treated as radical, less influential, and often out of step with the official categories that conservative modernization has already locked into place? Those questions set the stage for shifting from who controls change to how forceful, bottom-up forms of change try to push back, and later, to a deeper discussion of oppression and anti-oppression as concepts rather than just tools in a policy fight.

children.title: What’s ‘left’ for the rest? – force of change

paragraphs.text: Progressive approaches to curriculum operate very differently from the conservative mechanisms Apple describes. While conservative modernization works through state standards, policy mandates, and top-down levers of control, progressive change tends to grow from the bottom up — classrooms, communities, and the lived experiences of students. Inequality, not efficiency, is the main barrier progressives are trying to address. That focus shapes their theory of change: if the roots of inequality live in everyday experiences, then change has to start there. The challenge is that these bottom-up efforts still unfold inside a system whose categories, metrics, and priorities progressives did not create.

A good example of this tension comes from the concept of equality itself. Neither Culturally Responsive Pedagogy nor Critical Pedagogy lays out a clear definition of what equality actually is, or what it would mean to “reach” it. These traditions focus on justice, critical consciousness, redistribution, and liberation; not equality as a final destination, nor a stable, measurable endpoint. That ambiguity is intentional, but it also makes it harder for progressive work to scale. In a system shaped by conservative modernization and corporate assessment metrics, improvement must look like something you can measure. So when a vision refuses to define its end-goal in measurable terms, it struggles to gain traction within the structures that demand exactly that.

This comes through clearly in one of the most recognizable progressive strategies: representation. A large portion of practical CRE and CRP work revolves around questions like: Whose voices show up? Whose perspectives are centered? How much of the curriculum reflects the students sitting in front of us? Tools like the Culturally Responsive-Sustaining Education (CRSE) scorecard are intentionally designed for this kind of evaluation. They help parents, teachers, and students identify where curricula exclude certain communities or reinforce dominant norms. In theory, this is a democratizing move. It invites the people closest to the learning environment to assess the curriculum themselves.

But representation as a reform strategy also carries a built-in limitation. It asks families and educators to locate inequity within a set of materials that were already built around the categories the dominant system considers important. When the scorecard asks parents to examine whether “female characters are substituted for male characters” (CRSE, 2020), it unintentionally reinforces the very binary categories it hopes to disrupt. It encourages evaluators to look for differences through the identity labels the system already recognizes: male/female, white/non-white, dominant/marginalized. Instead of destabilizing these categories, the tool has to use them to prove they’re limiting.

This isn’t a critique of the scorecard itself, it’s a reflection of the landscape progressives are forced to operate in. Conservative modernization invites certain kinds of change, but only when that change ultimately keeps the existing structure intact. In Apple’s terms, conservatives “reform” to preserve: they accept new policies, new language, even new forms of accountability, so long as the underlying logic of standardization, competition, and hierarchy remains untouched.

Progressives don’t have that luxury. Their reforms aim to disrupt the logic itself, but the tools available to them are built inside the system they’re trying to challenge. In practice, that means progressive change often ends up using the same categories, evaluative frameworks, and measurement tools that created the problem in the first place. It becomes an attempt to fix broken logic with more of the same broken logic — not because the ideas are flawed, but because the system forces them to speak in its terms in order to be seen as “credible” or “legitimate.” These are the scaffolds on a crooked tower.

Anti-racist pedagogy and culturally responsive teaching are intentionally expansive. They push toward fluidity, complexity, and identities that are always in motion. But the structures they’re working within were built during the rise of the yeoman farmer, forged in the Industrial Age, and now refined in the Corporate Era — an era defined by efficiency, categorization, and measurement. Those habits didn’t disappear. Schools still inherit a logic that sorts, labels, and compares. It’s built to make differences legible, because legibility is what the system knows how to quantify.

This is one of the main reasons anti-racist pedagogy often falls short of its potential at scale. The ideas aren’t weak; the system is rigid. It reframes broad concepts of identity as boxes to check. It treats representation as an output rather than a relationship. In trying to repair the curriculum, progressive tools end up relying on the same categories of difference that the dominant system relies on — categories shaped by corporate-era notions of efficiency and evaluation.

This becomes a structural paradox: bottom-up change has to become visible to the top before it can grow. But the moment it becomes visible, it becomes limited. In the progressive view, change is relational, iterative, and built through shared experience. Inequality remains the biggest obstacle, and addressing it requires tools that push against rigidity. Yet because conservative modernization defines the official channels of “valid” change, progressives often have to use those same channels to justify their work. Their reforms can be powerful, but their power is always partially reshaped by the system that receives it.

children.title: If we misunderstand who moves change, we will misunderstand how to move it ourselves.

paragraphs.text: I hope you do not confuse this chapter as labeling curriculum as political, but that political dominance is just one major factor which shapes society. In a way, we are all responsible for change in curriculum. Theorists have their role to play; educators have theirs. Those logics act as the “middle man” between theory and practice. Unless we see how those forces interact, how they reinforce, distort, resist, or redirect one another, we cannot design a curriculum that is capable of doing anything more than repeating the patterns of its moment.

Curriculum reform so often fails to live up to its promises. Not because theorists lack vision, or because teachers lack skill, but because change is always filtered through structures and assumptions inherited from earlier periods. If Dewey struggled in the Industrial Age and Tyler was reshaped by the Corporate Age, it should not surprise us that today’s justice-oriented work is contending with the deeply embedded logic of conservative modernization. This positions us to imagine a curriculum that does not simply react to the forces around it, but actively reshapes how those forces are understood.

Educational change has never belonged to one group, one theorist, or one political camp. Change moves through a complicated chain of influence: society, theorists, institutions, politics, classrooms. Every link in that chain shapes the others. Dewey responded to the Progressive Era, Tyler codified the logic of the Corporate Era, and Apple diagnosed how conservative modernization now sets the boundaries of large-scale reform. Each of them reveals the same pattern: society shifts first, and curriculum follows. But curriculum also pushes back, often reframing the very social forces that helped produce it.

Together, these stories make one thing clear: there is no single architect of curricular change. There is instead a constant push and pull between society and schools; between theory and practice; between the foundations of the past, demands of the present, and the possibilities of the future. Sometimes conservative forces steer the channels through which official change is allowed to flow. Sometimes progressive energy disrupts those channels from below. But neither side determines everything. Curriculum lives in the tension between the two.

One question that remains to this day is a difficult question to ask: How does change happen? When a theorist designs a new framework, structure, or ‘curriculum,’ do college professors begin right away to teach the next generations of teachers? Or is change in education just more of an echo of current opinions where change? Do curriculum theorists have power, sway, or influence at all, or do theorists just have ideas of the time that they're able to translate into writing? I believe the answer is both because society was heading in that direction, and because theorists’ are valued as authorities when designing a curriculum.

John Dewey’s publishing journey predates the Spanish-American War – a war generally thrown in to a broader unit and tossed aside by US history curriculums. This War marked a major turning point in the global standing of the United States. At this point, the entirety of the “unclaimed” Western Hemisphere had been annexed by the United States or neighboring European-originated nations. This wasn’t satisfying enough for Americans, so they upgraded their tactics to imperialism. After pushing Europe mostly out of the West, and defeating Spain in the Spanish-American War, the United States stepped up to the rank of global partner.

Industrialization had spread across the states as the dominant economic opportunity for the working class by the end of the 19th century. Wartime manufacturing propelled the economy, benefiting the rich and powerful investors and manufacturers. By the turn of the century, the wealth gap continued to grow, and with it did power and corruption. Our industrial powerhouse made our presence indispensable when the British called on our help to fight the Germans in The Great War. Two years into US involvement, Dewey publishes Democracy and Education where he modernizes Jefferson’s citizenry purpose of education. In Dewey’s view, the purpose of education is to foster a continuously adapting and evolving democratic society where individuals are educated to participate in and contribute to their community.

children.title: WHO DOES NOT HAVE THE POWER?

paragraphs.text: Kevin Kumashiro offers one of the most widely cited frameworks for understanding oppression in educational contexts. His analysis begins from a clear premise: schools are not neutral environments. They are shaped by the same hierarchies, assumptions, and power dynamics that structure the broader society. For Kumashiro, addressing oppression in education requires attending to both the external structures that produce harm and the internal dispositions that sustain it.

He identifies two primary approaches. The first focuses on improving the experiences of students who are Othered, meaning those who are marginalized or oppressed in and by mainstream society. This approach confronts the visible forms of oppression: differential treatment based on race, gender, sexuality, or class; harassment, exclusion, and the deliberate withholding of resources. The second approach examines the assumptions and expectations educators carry about who students are or should be. This is the domain of the hidden curriculum. The harm that arises not from overt mistreatment but from the unstated beliefs that shape how a teacher interacts with a student before a word is spoken. Racial stereotypes, gendered expectations, heteronormative assumptions, and assimilationist beliefs operate below the surface of policy and produce harm even in the absence of malice.

Kumashiro further argues that oppression is not reducible to individual acts of prejudice. It is multiple, situated, and produced through the interaction of external treatment, internal ways of knowing, structural forces, ideologies, and discursive repetition. A student’s experience of oppression is not simply the sum of bad encounters, it is the accumulation of systems, narratives, and assumptions that together define what that student is expected to be.

This is genuinely important work. It moved the conversation beyond blaming individual teachers or specific curricula and toward recognizing oppression as systemic, layered, and often invisible to those who benefit from it.

NOTE: Source material: paras 259–261 from your current draft. I’ve expanded and smoothed the presentation but kept your characterization of Kumashiro. You’ll want to double-check the direct quotes against Troubling Education to make sure I haven’t drifted from his exact language.

Despite this nuance, Kumashiro’s framework orbits a particular axis. He identifies oppression by first establishing a dominant norm (white, male, heterosexual, middle-class, able-bodied, Christian) and then defining everyone who deviates from that norm as Other. The majority of students, he writes, are those who are not members of the dominant group: students of color, women, queer students, students with disabilities, students from non-Christian backgrounds, students from working-class families. Anyone who deviates from the established center, even slightly, is classified as an Other whose oppression must be addressed.

This approach has obvious strengths. It names real patterns and gives educators a vocabulary for recognizing who is harmed and how. But it also installs a structural limitation that shapes everything built on top of it. Oppression, in this framework, is always measured relative to a fixed center. The dominant group sets the benchmark, and everyone else is defined by their distance from it. The identity categories (race, gender, sexuality, class, ability) are treated as stable axes along which Otherness can be plotted. And the dominant group itself is implicitly positioned as the un-oppressed baseline, the reference point from which all deviation is measured.

This is where the framework encounters its own ceiling. Because true equality is a utopia individually held, it cannot be realized in practice since each person’s version of equality is shaped by their own experiences and cognitive reality. Any framework that defines oppression relative to a single dominant norm will be structurally incomplete. It can describe oppression within the categories it recognizes, but it cannot account for oppression that falls outside them, oppression that operates between them, or oppression that is produced by the act of categorizing itself.

NOTE: Your comment (Comment 0): "Is visible the right word? It’s to eradicate a norm because there is no concept of norm because there is no difference. This is obviously impossible." You’re right that full eradication is impossible. The paragraph above handles this: true equality is individually held and unrealizable. What follows is the question of what to do given that impossibility. Kumashiro’s answer: identify the dominant norm and advocate for the Other. Your answer (coming in Section B): shift the denominator from identity categories to cognitive self-awareness.

Kumashiro’s work is certainly profound, and my critique should not be read as a dismissal. It is true that each of the identifiers he names (whiteness, maleness, heterosexuality, wealth) carries a documented history of dominance and a measurable set of structural advantages. The patterns are real. But the question I want to ask is whether the analytical frame through which those patterns are examined might itself be contributing to the problem it diagnoses.

If the aim of anti-oppressive pedagogy is to reduce the harm caused by imposed identity, then perhaps it would be worth investigating whether that aim can be served by an approach that does not begin from identity at all.

NOTE: Source material: paras 258, 262–263 from your current draft. The last sentence is your pivot question, adapted from para 263: "Would it be wrong to shift the focus over to generalized oppression rather than narrowly focus on specific groups?" I’ve reframed it to be less tentative since you’ve committed to the argument.

Kumashiro is not alone in organizing oppression around identity. The entire landscape of anti-oppressive education operates through the same basic move. Anti-racist pedagogy, culturally responsive teaching, critical pedagogy, disability studies, queer theory… identify a marginalized group, examine the structures that marginalize them, and design interventions to disrupt those structures. The categories differ. The logic does not.

This shared logic creates a shared vulnerability. If anti-oppression frameworks define oppression through identity categories, and those identity categories are themselves socially constructed, then the frameworks are structurally dependent on the very constructions they aim to dismantle. Anti-racist pedagogy cannot operate without the concept of race. Gender-inclusive education cannot operate without the concept of gender. Disability advocacy cannot operate without the concept of ability. In each case, the tool of liberation requires the continued existence of the category it seeks to liberate people from.

This is not a reason to abandon those frameworks. They have produced real, measurable progress. Integration, visibility, representation, legal protection. None of these would have been possible without the deliberate identification of oppressed groups and the organized effort to address their specific harms. But it is a reason to look underneath the frameworks and ask a more fundamental question: what is oppression before it gets sorted into categories?

Racist and anti-racist theories, despite their opposing intentions, share a structural assumption. Both treat race as the denominator of the equation. For racist theories, race is a natural ordering that justifies hierarchy. For anti-racist theories, race is a social construction that must be confronted and dismantled. But in both cases, race must remain the organizing principle in order for the theory to function. If race were removed from the equation entirely, reduced to zero, the equation breaks. Both frameworks depend on the category’s continued relevance.

The same structural dependence holds for gender, sexuality, class, and ability. Each framework requires its category in order to do its work. This is not a flaw in any individual framework. It is a feature of the approach itself. Identity-based analysis can only see what identity-based categories make visible.

What it cannot see is what lies beneath the categories. The mechanism that produces imposed identity in the first place. The cognitive process by which a society decides what differences matter, assigns meaning to those differences, scales that meaning into institutions, and then treats the result as reality rather than construction. If that mechanism could be named, examined, and taught, it might offer something the category-based frameworks cannot: a response to oppression that does not depend on the perpetuation of the very categories oppression feeds on.
Naming that mechanism is the next step.

NOTE: This is the bridge into Section B (Cognitive Oppression: The Framework). The reader has now been given: (1) a fair presentation of Kumashiro, (2) a clear identification of the structural limitation, (3) the shared vulnerability across all identity-based frameworks, (4) the denominator metaphor from your current draft (para 293), and (5) a forward-pointing question that makes them want to turn the page. The tone is respectful but firm. You’re not attacking anyone. You’re asking what’s underneath.

NOTE: Your comment (Comment 8) on the outline: "True accurate reality cannot be perceived or known by human consciousness. That would require omnipotence. Instead, we form constructs to make sense of our understood realities. And the ones that make more sense to the most people (the two wolves), or the ones pushed by the dominant norm to benefit their place in reality, that is what becomes Jim Crow or Anti-Racism." This insight gets its full treatment in Section B (the scalability bridge). It doesn’t belong here in A.3 because the reader doesn’t have the consciousness framework yet. But it’s the exact idea that B.2 will develop.

NOTE: Your comment (Comment 13): "Metacognition is not natural. It’s not easy. And it’s not taught." I’d hold this for the very end of the chapter (Section E). It could be the closing line of the entire oppression section. It’s too powerful to spend early.

If oppression is not best understood through the categories it inhabits, then what is it? Start with the simplest possible case. Imagine a single consciousness, alone. No other mind exists. There is no language being imposed, no identity being assigned, no narrative about what this consciousness is supposed to be. There is experience, but there is no oppression, because there is nothing external shaping what this consciousness is allowed to think, feel, or imagine about itself.

Oppression, then, is not a feature of consciousness itself. It is a feature of consciousness in relation. The possibility of oppression begins the moment another consciousness exists and interacts with the first. Not because contact is inherently harmful, but because no two consciousnesses can fully access each other’s reality. Every attempt at communication, every shared experience, every act of meaning-making between two minds involves translation, filtering, and loss. What I intend is never exactly what you receive. What you understand about me is always a construct, assembled from your own prior experience, applied to signals I gave you, shaped by everything you already believe.

This is not yet oppression. This is the epistemic condition of being human. Two people who cannot fully understand each other are not oppressing each other. They are simply limited. Epistemic limitation is the precondition for oppression, but it is not the same thing. A conversation where both parties misunderstand each other is not oppressive. A relationship where neither person fully grasps the other’s inner world is not oppressive. These are the ordinary costs of being a mind that can only see out of its own eyes.

NOTE: This directly addresses your Comment 4 ("Am I conflating oppression with fairness?"). No. Fairness is a judgment made within a shared framework. Epistemic limitation is a neutral condition. Oppression is what happens when the limitation becomes directional, when one reality gets imposed on another. The distinction between limitation and oppression is the load-bearing wall of B.1.

Oppression begins when the interaction between consciousnesses stops being a mutual limitation and becomes a directional imposition. When one consciousness’s version of reality is treated as the version. When the definitions, categories, and meanings that one mind (or a collection of minds) uses to make sense of the world are applied to another mind without that mind’s participation, awareness, or consent. Oppression is what happens when your reality is defined for you.

This definition is deliberately broad. It does not confine oppression to race, gender, sexuality, class, or ability. Those are channels through which imposed meaning travels, but they are not the mechanism itself. The mechanism is the imposition of meaning onto a consciousness that did not choose it and may not even be aware it is happening. A child told she is "not a math person" has had a piece of her cognitive reality defined for her. A teenager absorbing the assumption that his worth is measured by his body on a football field has had a piece defined for him. A student in a school where only one version of history is taught has had an entire architecture of meaning installed before she had the tools to evaluate it. None of these require a racial or gendered lens to identify. All of them involve the same mechanism: an external meaning arriving and settling into a consciousness as though it were self-evident.

The scope of this mechanism has no outer edge. Kumashiro draws a boundary around identifiable groups: race, gender, sexuality, class, ability. Those boundaries are useful for the work his framework does. But the mechanism of imposed meaning does not respect those boundaries. A style of facial hair can carry imposed meaning after a dictator wears it. A regional accent can carry imposed meaning about intelligence. A lunch table can carry imposed meaning about social worth. These are not equivalent in severity to centuries of institutionalized racism, but they operate through the same cognitive process: a pattern of meaning, observed by multiple consciousnesses, is assigned to something, and that assignment begins to define what the thing is allowed to be.

This is why the sources of cognitive oppression cannot be listed and closed. Systems and law impose meaning; culture and norms impose meaning; other individuals impose meaning. Your own unexamined mind imposes meaning on itself, recycling inherited narratives as though they were original thoughts. Nature imposes meaning the moment a culture interprets a physical fact and decides it matters. To attempt a complete taxonomy of these sources would be to repeat the error this framework is designed to avoid. It would draw a boundary around the boundless and declare everything inside it the territory.

At the individual level, cognitive oppression manifests through three channels. There is internalized oppression, in which a consciousness constrains itself through unexamined beliefs, inherited narratives, and cognitive habits it did not choose. There is externalized oppression, in which a consciousness projects its own constraints onto others through communication, assumptions, and the unconscious filtering of meaning. And there is interpersonal oppression, in which the externalized constraints of others enter a consciousness and reshape its internal reality. These three compartments are the only pathways through which cognitive oppression can move. Every form of identity-based oppression (racism, sexism, homophobia, ableism) operates through all three. The identity category names the content, the compartment names the mechanism.

NOTE: The three compartments are introduced here as architecture, not fully developed. Section D expands each one with philosophical depth after the case study gives the reader concrete examples to anchor the abstractions. The ratio here should be roughly one paragraph of definition, then move on.

If cognitive oppression begins with two consciousnesses, it does not stay there. Understanding how it moves from the private interior of a single mind to the public architecture of a society is essential; because without that bridge, the framework appears to describe only individual psychology. Jim Crow was not individual psychology. It was law, violence, and institutional design. A theory of cognitive oppression that cannot account for Jim Crow is a theory that has not earned the right to replace the frameworks it critiques.

With only two consciousnesses, there is disagreement but not domination. Neither mind can impose its version of reality as the version, because there is no third party to validate the imposition. If one is physically stronger and takes the other’s food, that is force, not oppression. Oppression requires something beyond force. It requires a meaning that accompanies the force and outlasts it. Not "I took your food because I could" but "you are the kind of being whose food is mine to take." That second statement is a definition of reality. It assigns an identity. It says something about what the weaker consciousness is. And for that definition to hold, it needs agreement from someone other than the person making it.

NOTE: This directly addresses your Comments 5-6 about consciousness A stealing B's food. Force without meaning is not oppression. Force with meaning ("you are the kind of being whose food can be taken") is oppression, but it requires validation through coalition. Otherwise it's just one person's assertion, and the other person can simply reject it.

A third consciousness changes everything. Now coalition is possible. Two minds whose realities happen to align more closely with each other than with the third can, without planning or malice, establish a shared definition of what is normal and what deviates from it. The classic formulation: two wolves and a sheep voting on what to eat for dinner. The sheep is not outvoted because of any inherent deficiency. The sheep is outvoted because the wolves share an appetite, and shared appetite at the scale of three becomes majority, and majority becomes the operating definition of what dinner is.

The wolves do not need to hate the sheep. They do not need to be aware that their vote constitutes an imposition. They simply share a cognitive reality (hunger, the assumption that dinner means meat) that the sheep does not share. Their aligned limitation becomes the sheep’s imposed reality. And on this question, the alignment is stable. But on a different question (where to sleep, whether to cross a river, how to respond to a storm) the coalitions might shift entirely. The sheep and one wolf might align against the other. At the scale of three, oppression is situational, fluid, and reversible. No one is permanently the oppressor or the oppressed.

Now scale from three to thousands. To millions. Something qualitative changes. When a cognitive constraint is shared by enough minds, it stops feeling like a constraint and starts feeling like truth. Yuval Noah Harari argues in Sapiens that human societies uniquely scale through shared fictions: myths, religions, currencies, legal systems, national identities. These fictions work not because they are true in any absolute sense, but because enough consciousnesses treat them as true simultaneously. A dollar has value because a sufficient mass of minds agrees it does. A border exists because enough people enforce it. A racial hierarchy persists because enough consciousnesses have inherited, internalized, and externalized the narrative that it is natural.

True, accurate reality cannot be perceived or known by any human consciousness. That would require omnipotence. What we have instead are constructs: working models of the world assembled from experience, filtered through bias, and tested against the constructs of others. The constructs that make sense to the most people, or the constructs pushed by those with the most power, are the ones that harden into institutions. A single person’s belief that a certain group is inferior is private and relatively powerless. When that belief is shared across a critical mass of minds, it becomes culture. When culture is formalized into rules, it becomes policy. When policy is backed by enforcement, it becomes law. When law is maintained across generations, it becomes the way things are.

NOTE: This paragraph directly integrates your Comment 7-8 from the outline: "true accurate reality cannot be perceived or known by human consciousness. That would require omnipotence. Instead, we form constructs to make sense of our understood realities. And the ones that make more sense to the most people (the two wolves), or the ones pushed by the dominant norm to benefit their place in reality, that is what becomes Jim Crow or Anti-Racism." Your words are the philosophical engine of this passage. I expanded and smoothed but the core insight is yours.

Jim Crow was not a departure from cognitive oppression. It was cognitive oppression at societal scale. The mechanism was identical to the wolves and the sheep: aligned cognitive limitations (the inherited belief that Black people were inferior) producing a shared reality (segregation) enforced by coalition power (the state). What made Jim Crow devastating was not that the mechanism was different from an individual’s private racial bias. It was that the scale was different. Millions of aligned minds, centuries of accumulated institutional reinforcement, and the full apparatus of legal violence made one set of imposed meanings inescapable for the people living inside them.

This is the bridge that identity-category frameworks cannot build on their own. They correctly identify the content of scaled oppression (race, gender, sexuality) but they describe the content without explaining the mechanism. A cognitive oppression framework can account for Jim Crow, heteronormativity, and ableism through the same process: epistemic limitations, shared and scaled, producing imposed realities. The content differs. The mechanism does not.
If the mechanism of cognitive oppression operates at every scale, from the interior of a single mind to the architecture of a civilization, then a difficult conclusion follows. Everyone is inside it.

To many, that statement may come across as dismissive; however, it is not a claim that everyone suffers equally. The manifestations of cognitive oppression are wildly, incomparably unequal. A Black man in 1950s Alabama lived inside a reality defined for him by centuries of aligned institutional power, enforced by law, backed by violence, reproduced in every school and courthouse and bus station he entered. A white teenager in a Kansas suburb who absorbs the narrative that he has "no culture" is also living inside a reality defined for him. Both are cognitively constrained by meanings they did not choose. The severity, the violence, the institutional weight, the material consequences are not in the same universe.

The claim is about mechanism, not about magnitude. Everyone’s cognitive reality has been shaped by forces external to them. Everyone has inherited narratives, assumptions, and definitions that arrived before they had the tools to examine them. Everyone lives inside some configuration of imposed meaning. But the configurations are not equivalent. Some are enforced by the full weight of historical institutions. Others are private, uncodified, socially invisible. The difference between them is scale: how many consciousnesses aligned around the same imposition, how long that alignment has been maintained, and how much institutional power enforces it.

Tracing the history of any single form of oppression linearly, as though it were a story of progress toward a fixed destination, obscures this. It assumes that the moral standards of the present moment are closer to some universal truth than those of the past. It treats equality as a dichotomy between two groups without accounting for the cognitive individuality of every person inside those groups. And it assumes, most dangerously, that the people identified as oppressors cannot themselves be oppressed, as though occupying one position on one axis of power exempts a consciousness from all others. Lincoln was the most powerful man in the country and he was controlled by events he could not see clearly enough to choose. That is not an equivalence with the people he failed to liberate. It is evidence that the mechanism operates everywhere, even at the top of the hierarchy, while the severity is concentrated at the bottom.

NOTE: Your three issues from paras 274-277 are woven into this paragraph rather than presented as a numbered list. The Lincoln reference is a brief forward gesture to the case study. It plants a seed without developing the full argument, which comes in Section C.3.

If cognitive oppression is universal in mechanism but unequal in manifestation, then the language used to describe it must capture both dimensions simultaneously. The traditional vocabulary (oppressor and oppressed, dominant and marginalized, privileged and disadvantaged) captures the inequality but misses the universality. It sorts people into fixed positions and implies that the people on the dominant side of the binary are not themselves constrained. The cognitive framework suggests a different vocabulary.

An overexplored identity is an identity that has been defined in excessive detail by forces external to the self. Society has already decided what your race means, what your gender implies, what your class predicts, what your body permits. The definition may be hostile or sympathetic, stigmatizing or celebratory. It does not matter. What matters is that the definition arrived before the individual had the cognitive tools to participate in constructing it. A black student in 2026 inherits an enormous, detailed, institutionally reinforced narrative about what "black" means. That narrative was assembled over centuries by millions of aligned consciousnesses. It was refined through law, literature, science, media, and schooling. It is inescapable in the sense that every interaction the student has with the world passes through it. The identity has been explored to exhaustion by everyone except the person living inside it.

An underexplored identity is the corresponding cost. It is the self-knowledge that never develops because the external narrative is so loud. When society has already provided a comprehensive definition of who you are, the cognitive space for discovering who you are on your own terms shrinks. The work of self-definition is preempted by the definitions already in circulation. A student whose racial identity has been overexplored by society may have an underexplored sense of herself as a thinker, an artist, a philosopher, a person whose value is not indexed to the category the world sees first. The overexploration crowds out the underexploration. The imposed meaning displaces the unmade meaning.

These terms apply universally. A white student in a homogeneous community may have an underexplored racial identity (no one has ever asked him to think about what whiteness means, so it functions as an invisible default) and an overexplored class identity (everyone in his town knows what it means to be working-class, and the meaning has been imposed on him through generations of economic narrative). A wealthy student at an elite school may have an overexplored achievement identity and an underexplored emotional one. The terms do not sort people into fixed bins. They describe the relationship between the meanings a society has imposed and the meanings an individual has not yet had the opportunity to construct.

This is the vocabulary that replaces the oppressor/oppressed binary without erasing the inequality it describes. A black student’s racial identity has been overexplored at a scale and with a violence that a white student’s has not. That difference is real, material, and historically specific. But both students are living inside cognitive realities that were defined for them, and both would benefit from the tools to examine those definitions. The question for curriculum is not which student is oppressed and which is not; the question is: what kinds of cognitive tools would allow any student, regardless of which meanings have been imposed on them, to see those meanings as meanings rather than as facts.

NOTE: This last paragraph is the bridge into the case study. It sets up the question that Section C will answer through evidence: what does it look like, historically, when people live inside realities defined for them? The Douglass-Lincoln material, the slave revolts, the doll test all become illustrations of overexplored and underexplored identity in action.

NOTE: Your Comment 10 from the outline (escaping overexplored identity, trailing off with "or...?") is deliberately not resolved here. B.4 defines the terms. The resolution (metacognition as agency within oppression, not escape from it) belongs in Section E. If you answer the "what do you do about it" question before the case study, the case study loses its argumentative weight.
NOTE: Comment 13 ("Metacognition is not natural. It’s not easy. And it’s not taught.") remains held for the final line of Section E.

children.title: Why Race, and Why Black and White

paragraphs.text: A framework is only as credible as its hardest test. If cognitive oppression theory can account for the deepest, most violent, most institutionally entrenched form of identity-based oppression in American history, it can account for anything lighter. If it cannot, then it is an abstraction that breaks on contact with reality.

Race in the United States is that test. Not because race is the only axis of oppression, nor because the Black and white binary captures the full complexity of racial experience in this country. It does not. Indigenous peoples, Asian Americans, Latinx communities, mixed-race individuals, and immigrant populations all navigate distinct and intersecting configurations of imposed meaning that a Black/white lens cannot represent. To collapse their experiences into a single case study would be its own act of imposition.

The narrowing is deliberate. The history of black and white racial formation in the United States is the most extensively documented, most structurally embedded, and most legally codified form of identity-based oppression in the nation’s archive. It stretches from the founding documents to yesterday’s headlines. It has been analyzed from every disciplinary angle: legal, sociological, psychological, economic, educational, literary. This makes it the strongest possible stress test, because if the cognitive oppression framework holds here, it holds in territory that every other framework has already claimed.

There is a second reason for going deep on race, and it is the more important one. The point of this case study is not to prove that racial oppression exists, that has been established beyond serious dispute. The point is to demonstrate what happens when you examine racial oppression closely enough that the category itself begins to fracture. Every question this section raises (who counts as black, what about individuality within the group, what about the cognitive differences between people on the "same side") becomes visible only when the analysis pushes past the category and into the consciousnesses living inside it. Those questions cannot be asked while race remains the denominator. They emerge precisely when it stops being one.

NOTE: This addresses your editorial note at para 268 and the narrow-lens justification at para 306. The full spectrum of racial experience is acknowledged in paragraph 2. The narrowing is justified on two grounds: documentation depth and the analytical purpose of breaking the container. The second justification is more original and more aligned with the spine.

For almost 250 years, the definition of who counted as a person in the United States was written, enforced, and maintained by people who excluded most of the population from the authorship. The Framers did not end the slave trade in 1789. They wrote a twenty-year postponement into the Constitution, deferring the question the way a consciousness defers the thoughts it is not yet equipped to confront. Decades accumulated. Compromises were struck. Decisions were made without the participation, and often without the consideration, of the people most affected by them.

The cognitive oppression of enslaved people was not partial. It was total. Their identities were assigned by others. Their physical movement was controlled. Their family structures were destroyed at the discretion of people who had legally redefined them as property. But the most complete dimension of this oppression was not physical. It was the foreclosure of the imaginable. For many enslaved Americans, the reality of bondage was not merely a condition they suffered. It was the boundary of what they could conceive.

On few occasions, some broke the boundary. In 1800, an enslaved Virginian named Gabriel organized an attempt to seize the state capitol and hold the governor hostage, including James Monroe, future president of the United States. In 1822, Denmark Vesey, an enslaved South Carolinian inspired by the Haitian Revolution, led another large-scale plot. Both failed. Both were betrayed by informants. And in both cases, the informants were not plantation owners, not free men, not people with any structural incentive to preserve the system. They were other enslaved people.

This is not a moral judgment on the informants, but rather evidence of what cognitive oppression looks like when it has scaled to the point of totality. The informants did not choose the master’s side in some calculated weighing of options. For many, the alternative was literally inconceivable. The reality they inhabited had been defined so thoroughly, for so long, by so many aligned consciousnesses, that the boundary between what was real and what was possible had fused. Freedom was not a suppressed desire. It was, for some, an idea that had no space in which to form.

That is the spine of this paper in its most extreme expression. Their reality was defined for them. Not by any single person, but by centuries of accumulated imposed meaning, scaled through institutions, reproduced through law, and internalized so completely that it functioned as cognition itself.

NOTE: Source material: paras 269-273 from your original draft. Trimmed from 5 paragraphs of historical detail to 4 tightly focused on cognitive evidence. The census data and Georgetown plantation detail are cut. Gabriel and Vesey are preserved but the emphasis shifts from the rebellions to the informants, because the informants are the evidence for the spine.

NOTE: This is the centerpiece. Organized around one question from the ironic inversion thesis: who was more cognitively free, the escaped slave or the President? Every detail included either answers this question or gets cut. Four beats: (1) different cognitive realities colliding, (2) Douglass's metacognitive liberation, (3) Lincoln's institutional and cognitive constraints, (4) the inversion.

If the informants represent cognitive oppression at its most total, Frederick Douglass represents a beginning of its disruption. He did not end this type of oppression because even Douglass, who fought his way out of physical bondage and constructed one of the most powerful public voices in American history, spent his life navigating a world whose definitions he could challenge but never fully escape.

Douglass’s cognitive liberation began before his physical liberation. When Hugh Auld forbade his wife from teaching Douglass the alphabet, arguing that literacy would "forever unfit him to be a slave," Auld inadvertently handed Douglass the foundational logic of his own freedom. The imposed meaning (you are property, you are not to read, you are not to think independently) was exposed as a meaning rather than a fact. Douglass saw the definition for what it was. He acquired literacy in secret and from that moment forward, he possessed something the informants who betrayed Gabriel did not: the cognitive tools to perceive his own oppression as an imposition rather than as reality.

The fight with Edward Covey completed what literacy began. Douglass called it the "turning point" of his life as a slave, the moment that "rekindled the smoldering embers of liberty" and "revived my sense of manhood." By choosing the risk of death over submission, Douglass performed a metacognitive act. He refused the imposed meaning of his body (that it existed for someone else’s use) and asserted an alternative meaning (that it was his, and he would rather lose it than surrender its definition to another consciousness). This was not political liberation. Douglass could not vote, could not hold office, could not walk into a white church. But it was cognitive liberation. The reality that had been defined for him was, from that point on, a reality he could see, name, and resist.

His views continued to evolve. In his early years as a public speaker, Douglass operated within a framework set by white abolitionists, proving his "humanity" in terms they already accepted. Freedom, in that phase, meant demonstrating that a Black man could reason, speak, and argue as well as a white one. The imposed meaning of race was not yet questioned, it was performed against. Douglass was swimming against the current, but he was swimming in the current’s own direction. Only later, after breaking with the Garrisonians and developing a broader vision of equality, did he begin to construct a cognitive framework that was genuinely his own. His evolution documents what metacognitive liberation looks like as a process: not a single revelation but a slow, iterative expansion of what a consciousness allows itself to imagine.

Abraham Lincoln presents the inversion. Here was the most powerful man in the country, the commander of armies, the signatory of the Emancipation Proclamation. And yet his cognitive reality was, in ways that mattered, more constrained than that of the man who had once been legally classified as property.

Lincoln could not imagine full racial equality. During his 1858 senatorial campaign, he stated explicitly that he was "not, nor ever have been, in favor of bringing about in any way the social and political equality of the white and black races." He proposed deporting emancipated Black Americans to Liberia or Latin America. He was not unusual in this. He was a product of a frontier upbringing, limited travel, and a society that had defined race for him long before he held any office. His cognitive reality on the question of black humanity had been shaped by the same scaling mechanism that produced the informants’ inability to imagine freedom. The difference was one of degree, not of kind. Lincoln’s reality was defined for him by his era. He could question parts of it (slavery is wrong) while remaining inside other parts (black people are not equal) without experiencing any contradiction, because the contradiction was invisible from inside the imposed framework.

The presidency made this worse, not better. Lincoln was, as Douglass later put it, "preeminently the white man’s President." His duty was to a divided electorate. He won with 39 percent of the popular vote. Nearly four million Americans were enslaved. The census counted them but their voices counted for nothing. Every decision Lincoln made had to be calculated against the possible loss of support from border states, Northern moderates, and a military that was not yet fighting for abolition. He admitted this openly. In a letter written a year before his death, he reflected: "I claim not to have controlled events, but confess plainly that events have controlled me." This is the language of a consciousness describing its own cognitive constraints. Lincoln could see that his reality was being defined for him. He could name it. But he could not, from inside the office, step outside it.

Douglass recognized this inversion and spent decades articulating it. After their first meeting in 1863, he wrote that he was "not satisfied" with Lincoln and his slow efforts at abolition. He saw Lincoln’s humility as a weakness rather than a strength: "He argued like an attorney. I wanted him to act like a commander-in-chief." But by the time of their second meeting in 1864, Douglass began to understand that Lincoln’s constraints were not moral failures. They were structural features of a consciousness embedded in institutional power. Lincoln was not free to prioritize abolition because his office required him to maintain the consent of people who were not yet ready for it. Douglass, who answered to no electorate and held no office, was free to demand what Lincoln could not yet deliver.

In his 1876 oration at the unveiling of the Freedmen’s Monument, Douglass completed the inversion. He called Lincoln "preeminently the white man’s President" and described black Americans as Lincoln’s "step-children, children by adoption." He noted that Lincoln’s opposition to slavery had its "motive and mainspring in his patriotic devotion to the interests of his own race." But then Douglass reversed himself. He argued that Lincoln’s very prejudices and caution were what allowed him to maintain the coalition necessary to eventually destroy slavery. Lincoln was "fettered" by duty, and that fettering was the condition that made liberation possible. The man who was less cognitively free was the one who, precisely because of his constraints, could move the institutional machinery that Douglass’s cognitive freedom alone could not reach.

Neither man’s experience can be captured by the labels that history has assigned them. "Black" does not explain Douglass. "White" does not explain Lincoln. "Abolitionist" does not capture either of them, since they meant fundamentally different things by it. "Oppressor" does not capture Lincoln, a man who suffered depression severe enough to require suicidal intervention, who may have suppressed his own sexuality, and who described himself as controlled by events. "Oppressed" does not capture Douglass, a man who turned down tea with the President because he had a prior engagement. The categories are containers, and these two consciousnesses exceeded them in every direction.

NOTE: Source material: paras 279-288 from your original draft, enriched with the Gemini research doc (Covey fight, literacy as 'pathway from slavery to freedom,' 1876 oration, 'step-children by adoption,' the three White House meetings, 'events have controlled me'). Trimmed from ~10 paragraphs to 10 here, which is slightly longer than the outline's 5-6 target. This is the centerpiece, and I think the material justifies the length. But if you need to cut, the most expendable paragraph is the fourth (Douglass's evolution from Garrisonian framework). The least expendable is the last (categories as containers). Your call.

Douglass and Lincoln demonstrate what happens to the concept of race when you examine two individuals closely enough. The categories dissolve into cognitive particularity. But the frameworks designed to address racial oppression depend on the categories remaining intact. This is not a flaw in any individual framework. It is a structural feature of identity-based analysis.

In the 1940s, Kenneth and Mamie Clark asked children to assign attributes to white and black dolls. White children preferred the white dolls and attributed negative qualities to the black ones. That was expected. It was the response of black children that altered American law. In integrated Northern schools, black children showed what the Clarks called a "fundamental conflict" of the ego. They were more evasive, more anxious, more likely to refuse to continue the experiment when asked to identify with the brown-skinned doll. Southern Black children, raised under explicit segregation, could state matter-of-factly that the brown doll was "ugly." They had accepted the hierarchy. Northern children, raised in an environment that told them they were equal while every structural signal told them they were not, were caught between two imposed meanings. The collision of those meanings produced not liberation but psychological crisis.

The doll test succeeded. It became a cornerstone of the legal argument in Brown v. Board of Education and contributed to the de facto end of legally enforced segregation in public spaces. But it succeeded by using the same mechanism it was measuring. The test required children to identify with a racial group. It asked them to assign meaning to skin color. It measured the damage of imposed racial meaning by imposing racial meaning and observing what happened. The instrument and the injury shared a structure.

Decades later, the pattern persists. Modern curriculum evaluation tools like the CRE Scorecard invite parents to examine whether their children’s materials place "non-white or female characters in the place of white male characters." To use the scorecard, a parent must first define what a non-white character looks like. They must identify racial stereotypes in order to assess whether the materials transcend them. They must think in terms of race to evaluate whether the curriculum has moved beyond race. The tool requires categorical thinking to measure whether categorical thinking has been overcome.

Consider the position of a parent using this scorecard to evaluate an eighth-grade reading of To Kill a Mockingbird. The novel is set in the Deep South during the Great Depression and presents race through a particular, narrow lens. To evaluate it using the scorecard, the parent must apply their own understanding of racial stereotypes to the text. A black parent and a white parent may identify different stereotypes. Two black parents may identify different ones. Two parents from the same household may disagree. The evaluation depends on the evaluator’s own cognitive reality, which is itself a product of every imposed meaning about race they have ever absorbed. The tool does not transcend the problem. It reproduces it at the level of the assessor.

None of this diminishes the progressive achievements of anti-racist pedagogy. Integration changed material realities. Visibility shifted cultural narratives. Representation opened doors that were previously sealed. The argument is not that these efforts are wrong. The argument is that they are structurally incomplete, because they treat the delivery vehicle (race as a category) as though it were the cargo (the mechanism of imposed meaning). Anti-racist pedagogy is swimming against the current of racial oppression. It is doing so courageously and with real results. But it is swimming against one current in an ocean that contains infinitely many.
