NOTE: Source material: paras 293-305 from your original draft. Consolidated from ~13 paragraphs to 6. The To Kill a Mockingbird hypothetical is condensed to one paragraph. The 'swimming against one current' metaphor from our conversation closes the section and connects back to the spine. The last sentence is the bridge to C.5.

children.title: What Breaks When the Container Breaks

paragraphs.text: This case study has gone deep enough into one category to see what it looks like from the inside. "Black" is not a single cognitive experience. Douglass, the informants, the Northern children, the Southern children, a free Black man in Boston in 1850 and an enslaved person in South Carolina at the same moment all lived inside the same racial category and inhabited radically different cognitive realities. "White" is not a single cognitive experience. Lincoln, the abolitionists who still denied black equality, the slaveholders, the Northern voters who supported the war but not emancipation, an indigenous chief who had never encountered a Black person. Each consciousness processed its racial position through its own accumulated network of experience, belief, and imposed meaning.

The boundary between black and white is itself unstable. How much black does a person have to be? The one-drop rule, the shifting census categories, the lived experience of mixed-race children who report not knowing which group to identify with. These are not problems for the cognitive oppression framework. They are evidence for it. The fact that the boundary cannot be cleanly drawn proves the category is imposed rather than inherent. If race were a natural kind, its edges would be discoverable. Instead, the edges shift with every generation, every region, every political moment, because the category is not a fact about bodies. It is a meaning applied to bodies by consciousnesses acting in concert.

The same logic fractures every other identity category. Gender is not one experience. Sexuality is not one experience. Disability is not one experience. Class is not one experience. The moment a framework defines an oppressed group, it has flattened the cognitive individuality of every person inside that group into a label. The label may describe a real pattern of imposed meaning. It does not describe the millions of different ways that meaning lands inside millions of different consciousnesses.

This is why this paper does not repeat the case study for gender, sexuality, class, or ability. Doing so would replicate the analytical structure it critiques. It would treat each identity category as requiring its own dedicated examination, which is the exact move that maintains the categories as primary units of analysis. The absence of a dedicated section on gender oppression or disability oppression is not an oversight but rather the argument in practice. One deep case study breaks the container. Once broken, the reader can see that every container breaks the same way, for the same reason, through the same mechanism.

What remains, then, is the mechanism itself. Exposed, named, and unattached to any single category. The next question is how it operates inside a single consciousness. Not historically, not across a population, but in the private interior where imposed meanings first settle and where, if anywhere, they might be examined.

NOTE: This is the transition into Section D (The Three Compartments Expanded). The case study has proven the framework through historical evidence. Section D turns inward: how does cognitive oppression work inside one mind? The reader moves from the macro (centuries of scaled racial oppression) to the micro (the three compartments operating within a single consciousness). The closing paragraph does this without announcing it.

NOTE: Total paragraph count for Section C: approximately 25 paragraphs of prose. C.1: 4, C.2: 5, C.3: 10, C.4: 6, C.5: 5. This is moderately longer than the outline's target but significantly shorter than your original draft, which ran to roughly 40+ paragraphs for the same material. The Douglass-Lincoln material (C.3) is the longest subsection because it carries the most argumentative weight. If cuts are needed, C.4 can lose the To Kill a Mockingbird paragraph (the CRE scorecard alone proves the point), and C.3 can lose the Garrisonian evolution paragraph (fourth paragraph).

None of this is new. Half a century before these pages were written, working with Brazilian peasants learning to read, Paulo Freire described the mechanism at the center of everything that has been argued so far.

Freire called it prescription. "Every prescription," he wrote, "represents the imposition of one individual’s choice upon another, transforming the consciousness of the person prescribed to into one that conforms with the prescriber’s consciousness" (Freire, 1970, p. 47). That is the spine of the argument above, stated in different language: oppression is what happens when your reality is defined for you. He saw the internalization: the oppressed "have internalized the image of the oppressor and adopted his guidelines" and exist as divided beings, "at one and the same time themselves and the oppressor whose consciousness they have internalized" (p. 47). He saw the horizontal violence that follows: the oppressed striking out at their own comrades, because "the oppressor exists within their oppressed comrades" and attacking them is an indirect way of attacking the oppressor within (p. 62). He saw the limit-situations: the boundaries of imposed reality that people accept as given until they perceive them as constructed, at which point what Freire calls the "untested feasibility" becomes visible (pp. 99–102). And he named the educational structure that reproduces the cycle: the banking model, in which teachers deposit information into passive students whose role is to "receive, file, and store the deposits" (p. 72).

Freire’s prescription is the spine. His internalization is internalized oppression. His horizontal violence is the cycle between externalized and interpersonal oppression. His limit-situations are overexplored identities. His untested feasibility is underexplored identity. His banking education is the content-first curriculum that American schooling has been running for 250 years. The root system is his.

NOTE: Comment 2 on the outline: you noted that Freire's line about knowledge as a gift "from those who consider themselves knowledgeable to those they consider ignorant" is almost impossible to disprove given the relational definitions. That observation is worth holding for Part 2, where it connects to your critique of assessment. The assessor always positions themselves as the knower and the student as the not-yet-knower. That's banking logic embedded in the evaluation structure.

Freire worked within a Marxist class framework in which the oppressor and oppressed occupy socioeconomic positions and the prescriber is always identifiable: the landowner, the colonizer, the ruling class. Liberation, for Freire, is collective and political, and the pedagogy is forged "with, not for, the oppressed" in their struggle to transform the concrete situation of domination. Everything in his analysis depends on the existence of a nameable oppressor and a definable class of oppressed people who can organize against that oppressor.

The mechanism he described, however, does not require his framework to operate. A student who absorbs the belief that she is "not a math person" has had her cognitive reality defined for her without a class-based prescriber. The meaning arrived through accumulated cultural signals, teacher expectations, peer comparisons, and standardized test results. No single consciousness authored the imposition. It scaled through the same process Freire describes (prescription, internalization, reproduction) but without a colonial or class structure to locate the source. If the mechanism is real, it operates everywhere that meaning is imposed, not only where an oppressor class can be named.

Freire also described the cycle of internalization and horizontal violence without formalizing it as a system. He saw that the oppressed internalize the oppressor’s image. He saw that this internalization gets projected outward onto comrades. He saw that the projection reproduces the original imposition. But he did not name the three channels (internalized, externalized, interpersonal) as the exhaustive set of pathways through which cognitive oppression moves. Formalizing them makes the mechanism diagnosable across any context, not only class-based ones, and eventually addressable through specific practices designed to interrupt each channel.

NOTE: Comment 5-6: you asked whether to introduce the axiometrica calculus / ontological dictionary vocabulary here. Recommendation: not yet. A footnote can signal that the formal architecture exists and will be developed in Part 2. Part 1 has enough new terminology. Let the reader absorb the three compartments and the cycle before adding the endosphere and the outer lens.

The most important departure is not analytical but purposive. Freire’s project is collective political liberation through praxis, which he defines as the inseparable unity of reflection and action on the world. For Freire, reflection without action is "verbalism" and action without reflection is "activism." Neither is authentic. He would ask of any metacognitive framework: where does the student act on the world? Where does internal examination become external transformation?

The honest answer is that external transformation is not the purpose. The project is self-emancipation from the self: the ongoing, never-finished work of examining the meanings imposed on your consciousness and making deliberate choices about which to keep, which to revise, and which to reject. A student who goes through this process and chooses to topple a fascist regime is no more successful than a classmate who goes through the same process and consciously chooses to remain a farmer. Both have examined the realities defined for them. Both have exercised cognitive sovereignty over their own thinking. The measure is not the action; the measure is whether the consciousness behind the action is one that has been examined or one that was installed.

Freire’s praxis is one form of examined engagement with the world. Conscious farming is another. Conscious artmaking is another. Conscious parenting is another. What they share is that the consciousness doing the farming, the art, or the parenting has examined the meanings imposed on it and made deliberate choices about which to keep, which to revise, and which to reject. A contexture builds that capacity. What students do with it is their sovereignty.

NOTE: Comment 10 flagged 'what they share is that the consciousness doing the farming...' as the most important line in this section, worth stress testing. Stress test: what about a student who develops metacognitive capacity and uses it to become a more effective propagandist? They've examined their meanings and chosen to impose meanings on others. Answer: the framework names deliberate externalized oppression (conscious imposition of meaning after examination) as the one act that the habits are designed to make visible and resistible. The farmer, revolutionary, and artist are all fine because their sovereignty does not require imposing on another consciousness. The propagandist is the edge case where cognitive sovereignty has been achieved but directed toward constraining others' sovereignty. That is the one place where the framework makes a value judgment: cognitive sovereignty exercised to eliminate others' cognitive sovereignty is self-contradicting.

NOTE: Comment 8: you noted that self-emancipation is not 'complete' but iterative. The map metaphor: you can never have a fully accurate map, only a more accurate one. Cognitive sovereignty is asymptotic. I've used 'ongoing, never-finished' in the prose and will add a footnote on 'sovereignty' as used here being a direction of movement, not a destination.

If cognitive oppression is a condition of consciousness in relation, then it must have mechanics. It must move through identifiable channels. And if it reproduces itself across generations, there must be a cycle. Freire described pieces of this cycle. What follows is an attempt to map the full loop.

The first stage is internalization. A consciousness absorbs imposed meanings without examining them. These may arrive from family, culture, media, schooling, or the accumulated residue of institutional history. The meanings settle into the cognitive architecture as though they are self-evident. Freire described this precisely: "So often do they hear that they are good for nothing, know nothing and are incapable of learning anything, that in the end they become convinced of their own unfitness" (p. 63). The student does not know she is carrying these meanings. They are not beliefs she holds. They are the lens through which she sees. Research in educational psychology confirms the reach of this process: internalized oppression is empirically linked to depression, anxiety, reduced self-esteem, and self-destructive behavior across multiple identity groups (David, 2013; David et al., 2019), and the mechanism operates across identity categories rather than within a single one (Mikuła et al., 2025).

The second stage is externalization. The consciousness, now carrying unexamined meanings, projects them outward through communication, behavior, assumptions, and unconscious filtering. A teacher who has internalized low expectations for a particular group of students externalizes those expectations through the questions she asks, the patience she extends, the opportunities she provides. She may not be aware she is doing it. The externalization is filtered through her own biases and arrives in the world as a new act of meaning-imposition. This is Freire’s "horizontal violence" generalized: not only the oppressed striking their comrades, but any consciousness projecting its unexamined constraints onto another. The direction is not fixed. A student who rolls her eyes, falls asleep, or raises her hand with performative eagerness is externalizing imposed meanings upward toward the teacher just as the teacher externalizes downward toward the student. The cycle does not respect hierarchy.

The third stage is institutional accumulation. When enough consciousnesses externalize the same imposed meanings, those meanings harden into structures. Policies, laws, norms, curricula, assessment systems, hiring practices. The structure persists independently of any single consciousness. A useful illustration comes from behavioral research. In an experiment frequently cited in organizational psychology, primates in a group were conditioned to avoid reaching for food by punishing the entire group whenever one individual tried. When every original member had been replaced, the new members continued to prevent each other from reaching for the food, though none of them had ever experienced the outside punishment. The behavior had become institutional. No living consciousness carried the original reason. The imposed meaning sustained itself.

NOTE: Comment 15-17: the monkey/ladder study. I've included it here in Stage 3 as an illustration of institutional accumulation without requiring a living author. The parallel to human institutions (redlining, content-first curriculum, heteronormative assumptions) is structural. The redlining map from 1935 still shaping neighborhood wealth in 2026 operates through the same mechanism at greater complexity.

The fourth stage is interpersonal re-entry. The institutional structure, now operating on its own momentum, imposes meaning on new consciousnesses. A child enters a school built on content-first assumptions, sorted by age-graded cohorts, assessed through standardized instruments. The school’s structure carries the accumulated cognitive constraints of every consciousness that built it. Those constraints enter the child as interpersonal oppression: other people’s externalized meanings, scaled through institutions, arriving as the new child’s internalized reality. The cycle restarts.

What the cycle reveals is how a single person’s private cognitive constraint becomes Jim Crow across centuries, and also how a single teacher’s unexamined assumption about "math people" becomes a student’s unexamined belief about herself across a single school year. The mechanism does not change. The scale does.

NOTE: Research note for citations: Steele & Aronson (1995) on stereotype threat is the empirical demonstration of Stage 4 (interpersonal re-entry). The awareness that a stereotype exists degrades cognitive performance even when the person does not believe the stereotype. That is institutional meaning entering an individual consciousness in real time. Gutierrez de Blume (2023) found that metacognitive awareness predicted decreases in implicit bias, which is empirical evidence that metacognition interrupts the cycle at Stage 2 (externalization). Both should be cited in the final version.

The cycle is self-sustaining. Without intervention, it reproduces itself. Each generation inherits the imposed meanings of the last, externalizes them, and passes them to the next. The question is where to break in.

Political intervention targets Stage 3. Pass a law. Change a policy. Restructure a system. Jim Crow did not end through metacognition. It ended through legislation, protest, legal challenge, and political organization. Anti-racist pedagogy, civil rights advocacy, disability rights movements: all of these target the institutional stage of the cycle, and all of them have produced real, material, life-altering results. Nothing in the argument above diminishes that work.

But political intervention alone is structurally incomplete. A law can end segregation. It cannot end the cognitive constraints that produced segregation in the first place. Those constraints persist inside individual consciousnesses, continuing to externalize through interpersonal channels, continuing to accumulate in new institutional forms. The cycle repairs itself unless it is also interrupted at the level of the individual.

Metacognitive intervention targets Stages 1 and 2. It gives a consciousness the tools to detect the imposed meanings it carries; to examine where those meanings came from and how they filter communication; to model how other consciousnesses carry different imposed meanings; and to construct new meanings through deliberate synthesis rather than unconscious inheritance. It does not eliminate oppression. It gives the individual agency within it.

NOTE: Comment 20-21: you noted that the metacognitive habits need introduction here, even if brief. The sentence above gestures at endospection (detecting imposed meanings), refraction (examining how they filter communication), exospection (modeling other consciousnesses), and synthesis (constructing new meanings). These are introduced functionally, not by name. A footnote (*) can list the formal terms: "These capacities correspond to the six metacognitive habits developed in Part 2: endospection, omnipere, constellare, refraction, exospection, and synthesis." This gives the reader a preview without requiring them to absorb the vocabulary yet.

Everyone is swimming in an ocean of imposed meaning. The ocean is infinite. Anti-racist pedagogy swims against one current. Disability advocacy swims against another. Class-based organizing swims against another. Each is necessary. Each addresses a specific scaled imposition. Metacognition does not swim against any particular current. Metacognition is learning how to swim.

No one escapes the ocean. A consciousness that knows it is in a current, knows the current’s direction, and can make deliberate choices about when to swim with it, against it, or across it still has not achieved total sovereignty over its reality, and never will. Total sovereignty would require omniscience. What it has achieved is something more modest and more durable: the capacity to see the current as a current rather than as the way water moves. That capacity is ongoing. It does not arrive and stay. It is practiced, lost, recovered, refined, and practiced again. It is more like fitness than like a diploma.

Douglass could not vote, could not hold office, could not walk into a white church. But his metacognitive capacity gave him the internal freedom to think beyond his material circumstances. That is what made him Douglass rather than one of the informants who betrayed Gabriel. Both were inside the same current. One was swimming.

children.title: Metacognition is not natural. It is not easy. And it is not taught.

paragraphs.text: For Freire, success is collective liberation: the transformation of the concrete situation of oppression through praxis. For a cognitive framework, success is different. A student who develops the capacity to examine the meanings imposed on her and joins a revolution has succeeded. A student who develops the same capacity and consciously chooses to farm has equally succeeded. A student who develops the same capacity and decides, after examination, that the values she inherited are the values she endorses has also succeeded. The measure is not the content of the choice. The measure is whether the choice was examined.

This is not relativism. It is not a claim that all choices are equally good. It is a claim that the cognitive capacity to examine one’s choices is a prerequisite for any choice being authentically one’s own. A contexture cannot determine what students will value. It should not try. But it can determine whether students have the tools to examine what they value and why. That is the scope of what schools can do. That is the boundary of the project.

NOTE: Comment 26: you flagged 'but it can determine whether students have the tools to examine what they value' for stress testing. The stress test: how do you assess this? How do you know the tools are working versus a student performing examination for a grade? This is the central assessment problem of Part 2. In Part 1, the claim is defensible philosophically: a contexture can build the conditions for examination. Whether it does in any given case is an empirical question that Part 2's assessment architecture must address. The claim here is about capacity, not verification.

NOTE: Comment 27-28: I've used 'contexture' instead of 'curriculum' in this subsection. You noted that calling it a curriculum dilutes the differentiation and risks it being absorbed as just another framework. Contexture signals the change of scope.

A system oriented around content coverage produces students who have absorbed meanings. A system oriented around metacognitive cogniscience produces students who can examine meanings. The first system is what American schools have been doing for 250 years. The second is what the remainder of this argument describes.

Conservative modernization sits at the choke points of curricular change. It controls the standards, the testing regimes, the accountability frameworks, and the language through which reform must justify itself. Progressive educators work within those channels or around them, bending the system’s own tools toward different purposes (representation scorecards, culturally responsive materials, anti-racist units) while accepting that the moment those tools become visible to the dominant system, they get absorbed, measured, and constrained by it. The mechanics of that power explain why reform so often fails to outlast its own moment: how it flows, who holds the levers, what happens when bottom-up change tries to move through top-down channels.
But power does not only operate through policy and infrastructure. It operates through something quieter and more pervasive: the ability to define what counts as real.

NOTE: This is the key transition. The Apple chapter was about institutional power (who controls the levers). This chapter goes deeper: who controls the meaning. Your recontextualization: conservative = a dominant who benefits from the system and promotes its continuance; progressive = a subdominant who does not benefit and requests change. That framing carries forward here, but the focus shifts from the political mechanics to the cognitive mechanics of how dominance actually works inside people’s heads.

If society is what changes curriculum, then what changes society? The values and experiences of individuals collectively form the values of a culture. But not equally. Those in positions of dominance do not simply hold more resources or louder microphones. They hold something more fundamental: the capacity to define the default. They determine what is considered normal, what deviations from that normal are tolerated, and which deviations are treated as threats. The conservative project Apple describes is not only a political coalition. It is an act of reality construction. A particular set of meanings about school, knowledge, success, and citizenship is asserted not as a choice but as a fact.

Those who do not benefit from the dominant arrangement experience this differently. They do not encounter the default as a neutral backdrop, they encounter it as a constraint. A set of definitions written before they arrived, applied to them without their participation, and enforced by systems they had no hand in designing. When a student is sorted into a category (by race, by ability, by language, by behavior) the sorting does not begin in the classroom. It begins in the accumulated cognitive history of every person and institution that shaped the category before the student ever walked through the door.

NOTE: Your comment on the outline (Comment 0) asked: "Who gets to decide how much (and what) differences are allowed in a society? The anti-racists think it’s them, and the billionaires think it’s them." That tension is exactly what this paragraph sets up. The answer that emerges over the chapter: nobody should get to decide, because the act of deciding is itself the imposition. Metacognition is the alternative — teaching people to examine the definitions rather than imposing better ones.

Below the level of policy and politics, a more fundamental question waits. What happens to the people who live inside a system where their reality has already been defined for them? How does a dominant norm become so embedded that it stops looking like a norm and starts looking like the way things are? And once it has, what would it take to make it visible again? Not politically. Cognitively.
To answer those questions, we have to look more closely at the concept of oppression itself. Not as a political label. As a condition of consciousness.

Despite surface differences such as funding or location, the foundational architecture of American public schooling is identical: age-graded cohorts, bell schedules, and the revolutions around the “Core Four” subjects. Nearly every elementary student is encouraged to learn basic math and how to read. In middle school, students are introduced to essay writing and scientific method. In high school, almost any student pursuing a higher education takes the SAT, ACT, AP/IB courses, or some other form of standardized test in order to be compared against thousands of others for college admissions.

Debates rage across party, region, and religion as to what content should or shouldn’t be taught. Often times a product of grouping-mentality, parents, students, or community members may assume active roles in the shaping of education or curriculum adoption. This is done in many ways, including board meetings, self/peer evaluations, or through contact with their child or child’s teachers/administrators. many cases, public schools have been forced to remove books, alter course content, or make structural changes. But these battles are often distractions; the debates remain endless and cyclical. There will always be aspects of the main, null, or hidden curriculum that promote oppression.

Due to the collective structure of assessment and evaluation of curriculum and of students, change tends to affect more than just the student asking for it. For instance, a parent demanding his daughter learns about the Rwandan Genocide for more than a brief mention in her world history class would imply the teacher modify her curriculum for the entire class. Perhaps they can offer more of a variety in terms of assignments given during that unit – but with objectives and state standards to assess for, alignment of multiple assignments might be difficult.

More tellingly, methods of differentiated learning increasingly rely on accommodations such as IEPs and 504s. The system attempts to scaffold students with 'learning disabilities' by assuming that any deviation from the dominant average is a deficit. But this reveals a structural flaw: Why does the 'regular' classroom require legal documentation to accommodate natural human variation? Again and again, the assumptions of a 'right' way to learn limit the opportunities for metacognition. It assumes that 'normal' learners are identical, and that those with different cognitive topologies must be retrofitted to the standard model.

A deaf or blind student would have tremendous difficulty passing assessments in the average US public school. Is there a physical internal difference in the capacity to think between someone who is deaf and someone who is not? Not necessarily. Aside from hearing, the barrier is not the math nor the literature, but the prescribed architecture of delivery and deterministic standardized assessments. We don’t need a system that accommodates exceptions; we need a system where cognitive variation is the assumption.

Assumptions about a "correct" schooling model prevent learners with physical or cognitive variabilities from success without segregation or accommodation. In a content-first curriculum, the implication of a "right" and "wrong" mentality oppresses perspective into a dichromatic lens. It challenges us to look for a middle ground, but there is no single fixed middle ground everyone can occupy; there are only overlapping, shifting shared understandings that must be consciously negotiated.

If experiences form the interconnected nodes of awareness, then the cognitive perception of an idea cannot be equally shared between two people. Therefore, the role of school is not to force students to meet in the middle, but to teach them how to bridge the gap, how to consciously update one’s reality autonomously – to learn how to learn.

If learning is about bridging realities rather than forcing everyone to meet in the middle, then communication becomes the key commodity in translating an idea or a thought from one’s own consciousness into one of the infinite modes of articulated expression. Traditionally, communication is measured in structured, often binary ways such as multiple-choice questions, essay rubrics, or an answer key. Because of objective and standard alignment, assessment differentiation can easily become inequitable. A teacher who allows assessment options to be submitted as an essay, podcast, or poem must create different ways of measuring a student’s ability to communicate achievement of an objective – often through communicating knowledge.

Every interaction consists of many forms of communication. Even without intentional effort, bodies are constantly ‘communicating’ with themselves through automatic processes. With little to no conscious consumption, one’s body communicates with itself to pump the heart, breathe, or blink. More commonly observed as communication, actions such as reading, writing, or speaking are forms of external communication. Intentional and unintentional facial expressions, systematic body language, or other “tells” can communicate subconscious emotion or thought. Metacognition itself is a form of internal communication.

In specific professional fields, strictly structured communication is not just preferable, it can be necessary. Collective agreements around “truths” provide emergency life-saving precision in surgery rooms. For a non-surgeon, the difference between a hemostat and a needle holder may mean nothing. But if a surgeon called for a hemostat to clamp a vessel and the scrub tech handed over the needle holder, the aggressive jaws could crush and macerate the delicate blood vessel, potentially causing more bleeding rather than stopping it.

The problem is not that strict codes exist, or even that structure, precision, and accuracy are core components of academic access. The reliance on memorization and correct answers as the only metric is what hinders metacognition. Schools become confused with operating rooms where scrub techs are assessed on accuracy under pressure. However, a patient’s surgery is equally dependent on the scrub tech’s ability to recognize a hemostat from a needle holder and the surgeons understanding of where, how, and why to use what tools when. We confuse the memorization of the tool (the hemostat) with the judgment required to use it.

Chemists, musicians, and bakers all communicate success in seemingly different ways. A chemist articulates success by publishing lab results in a peer-reviewed journal documenting her experiment’s hypothesis, results, and analysis. A musician has a different type of flexibility in terms of communicating alignment toward an objective. The variation of communication style is displayed in how a piece is played, sung, composed, or arranged. Musicians can communicate their perspectives and individual, autonomous distinctiveness by taking liberties in aspects of rhythm, pitch, transposition, remix, or covers. Much like snowflakes, a song cannot possibly be played the same way live twice. The timing, hertz frequencies, and many other tiny variables make it so that even the most consistent musician can never exactly recommunicate their reality. These differences become even clearer when both are asked to follow the same “recipe” in a space like a baking contest.

Both the chemist and musician might go about communication in a very different way. A chemist, whose day-to-day work consists largely of precise measurements and expected chemical-reaction outcomes, would be more likely to stick to a strict interpretation of the recipe, attempting little variation. The musician, whose life consists of a more abstract form of communication, may take more liberties by adding their own flair to the recipe. In a metacognitive curriculum, these varied modes of communication are not just outputs to be graded, but starting points for students to notice, name, and refine how they learn.

Just as disciplines differ in how they communicate success, school subjects are not as cleanly separated as their schedules suggest. A student in a high school biology class might think that his history class shares no overlap with his lab assignment on hierarchies and the classification of organisms. History class, meanwhile, covers the great ancient empires of the old world. The student will go from his lab to his lecture on the collapse of the Roman Republic and patrician off the knowledge from biology. There is no inherent opportunity, invitation, nor incentivization for the student to draw connections between the two fields.

Biology and history both invite learners to see and question hierarchies, whether in the classification of organisms or in the structuring of societies and empires. Chemistry’s themes of cause, effect, and reaction parallel historical chains of action and consequence. When we limit content to tightly bounded subject silos, we implicitly teach that each discipline’s way of thinking and communicating is fixed. That is a static cognition belief, not a metacognitive habit.

Most communication is subtle, unintentional, or quickly forgotten. Not many people are blessed, or cursed, with a perfect photographic memory. Remembering your last conversation exactly word for word is nearly impossible and not often attempted. However, you might remember the topic of the conversation, emotions you felt during it, or a task or takeaway. After a time, subtle cues and unintentional modes of communication during the conversation become as blended together as the actual verbatim words. Metacognition is what lets us step back from those blended impressions and ask how we made sense of them, why we reacted the way we did, and how our patterns of thinking might change next time.

Cognition is innate and inherent for homo sapiens. Life’s unique gift of awareness conducted by memory allows for cognition’s existence. Interpreting literary text by the words rather than the theme, engaging in a conversation without focusing on anything aside from the exchanging of words, or solving 2 + 2, are all forms of cognition. It is the ability to realize, understand, and recall memories and knowledge. Metacognition adds another layer: it is the ability to notice and shape one’s own thinking – to understand how ideas, thoughts, and abstract concepts connect to everything else, and to decide how to navigate those connections. It’s the ability to see the lines connecting the various nodes in one’s awareness and to adjust navigation along those lines.

Over the past few decades, metacognition has generally been defined as people’s knowledge of and control over their own thinking. Introducing the term to pedagogical research, J.H. Flavell describes metacognition as “knowledge and cognition about cognitive phenomena,” or in other words, cognitions about one’s own cognitions. Schraw and Dennison build on this by distinguishing knowledge of cognition (being aware of how you think) from regulation of cognition (planning, monitoring, and evaluating how you are thinking). Veenman and colleagues similarly highlight planning, monitoring, and evaluation or judgment as core metacognitive skills that influence how students approach tasks and how well they perform.

Neuroscience has started to map this capacity to specific brain systems: research on decision-making suggests that regions in the anterior and rostrolateral prefrontal cortex are especially involved in monitoring confidence and accuracy, or more simply in how we “think about” our own judgments. In education, meta-analyses like Hattie’s Visible Learning and later work on learning strategies consistently show that metacognitive strategies (knowing how you learn, monitoring your understanding, adjusting strategies) have a sizable positive impact on student achievement. In other words, metacognition is not just a nice add-on; it is one of the main engines of effective learning.

Acknowledging the similarities and differences in the baking results between the chemist and the musician is a form of cognition. In a classroom setting with a student performing at a high level in chemistry and a student performing at a high level in orchestra, their skills and forms of communication should not necessarily be assessed the same way. In society, schools included, there are a set of universal agreements, like 1.01 cups of flour being essentially the same as 1.00 cups when baking cookies. But if the musician decided to use .75 cups flour and an extra 25% of sugar, that’s a cognitively significant variation from the recipe. If the baking evaluation were based on alignment to a rubric with indicators of exact recipe usage, the musician would have points taken off and the chemist would not.

A metacognitive evaluation would not assume the musician did anything wrong; rather, it would evaluate the musician’s opportunity to learn about their own learning. Why did the student make that choice? Was it because they couldn’t read the recipe correctly? Was it because they felt the best expression of their baking communication would be a counternormative take on brownies? Perhaps it was out of deliberate curiosity to invent something new. A traditional evaluation would treat the deviation as an error; a metacognitive evaluation treats it as data. The point is not to reward or punish the choice, but to surface and refine the thinking behind it.

Of course, stakeholders at the other end of communication also matter. Much like the example with surgeons, it would be impractical to refrain from merging your reality with that of others. In an evaluation on baking for a specific type of customer, the assessment might look different. Perhaps it is an interdisciplinary experiment to construct a cake in the same style as the Framers constructing the Constitution. In that case, a decision to design a marble cake in the spirit of federalism might carry more weight than the result. In other circumstances, the chemistry of the cake might carry more weight in assessment than the artistic parameters.

What objective would you be assessing for in this case? What state standard would be achieved by this evaluation? One answer might be that you are assessing students’ understanding of how structural compromises shape both the stability and fragility of a system. But there is no neat standard labeled “experiences the ethical instability of representational injustice through baking.” That gap exposes how content-anchored objectives struggle to capture metacognitive and conceptual work that spills across disciplines.

Certain conceptual objectives are necessary to ensure metacognition is being activated and time is not spent unproductively. But these objectives should not be set in stone. They should evolve throughout the entire process of the assignment, lesson, unit, course, or educational journey. Unfortunately, these types of experiments are often considered distractions from core knowledge because they might take too much time away from other information. Another critique has been shouting through the cracks: if the dominant traditional model of curriculum is “working” for most people, and IEPs and 504s provide scaffolded support, why shift evaluation to allow for differentiated forms of communication and objectives if everyone would still have to do the same thing?

The answer is that “doing the same thing” is not the same as “learning in the same way.” A system that treats accommodations as legal exceptions to a fixed path may help more students reach the test, but it still withholds the chance to understand and redesign their own patterns of thinking. Metacognition is not an extra support layered onto a content-first curriculum; it is the work of becoming aware of and responsible for one’s own learning.

The differentiation of cognition and metacognition has been justified here. Content proves to be a major limiting factor in metacognitive exploration. Corporate-era logic, with its emphasis on fixed objectives, efficiency, and accuracy, hinders individuals from proving their worth in their strongest modes of communication. If curriculum can no longer be organized around stable content, it has to be organized around something else: the ways students learn, revise, and communicate their thinking. So if not content, then it should focus on metacognition. But what would a curriculum that supports metacognition look like? What provides solutions to the taped scaffolds of the crooked buildings?

children.title: Nature vs Nurture | Instinct vs Reflex | Biology vs Society | Evolutionary substrate vs Cultural shaping

paragraphs.text: Reflex and instinct are quintessential attributes for life’s survival. In fact, nearly all thought is either of the two: breathing, pumping blood, and even the drives of hunger, thirst, or lust. Have you ever shaken a ketchup bottle or lifted up a box to guess how much (or little) was left in the container? Or have you ever been in the driver’s seat of a car and been surprised by your location after not remembering the last 10 miles? How often do you respond to a question without taking the time to think about what is actually being asked? And of course, no one is immune from some degree of emotional influence on decision making.

These attributes did not randomly appear one day. Some are inherited biologically. Without hunger, a mortal species would have no incentive to eat; without lust, it would die out. Over millennia, bodies that handled hunger, threat, and pursuit a little better than their neighbors left more descendants. The substrate isn't a memory of any event your ancestors lived through. It's the leftover of which mutations happened to work.

But biology is only half the story. The other half is Geist: Hegel's name for the way culture passes itself across generations through language, institution, ritual, and example. Geist takes the substrate and shapes it into specific behaviors. Hunger is biology; what counts as food is Geist. Hand-eye coordination is biology; the existence of touchdown passes is Geist. The bias to learn fears of fast-moving things is biology; the specific dread of rats is mostly Geist.

Both run beneath awareness. The "nurture vs nature" debate treats them as competing inputs, which is partially correct, but it overlooks the more pressing fact: the result of an experience is a self that acts before it watches itself act. The substrate breathes. Geist shapes the craving. You¹ (the actor, the answerer, the reflex) moves. You² (the watcher) arrives late, if at all, and asks what just happened. Endospection allows You² to show up earlier and more often.

While our survival depends on reflex and instinct, our evolution depends on metacognition. Autopilot behaviors inherently signal a divorce between the first-person observer and their own agency. Most of the time, these behaviors are irrecoverable. You may have driven the last 10 miles without realizing it, snapped back into awareness mode, and not realize you ever ‘zoned out.’ How many breaths of air have you taken in your life? If you focus on your breathing while meditating, or are out of breath from a run, it’s not difficult to notice the lungs expanding and deflating. But where does that feeling go when you think about something else? The lungs still expand and deflate, your eyes still blink when you don’t think about them, you still drove those 10 miles.

It is only when you think to yourself “what just happened” that the existence of that event becomes real. Here’s a simple experiment. If you ever fall into the trap of Doomscrolling, set an alarm for 5 minutes and don’t look at it. Once that alarm rings, try and remember what reel you watched 2 swipes ago. You may remember it, but it is lost without the intentional effort to remember or recall it. This example is an experiment to practice analyzing your behaviors and the first step in practicing Endospecture.

The awareness of the autopilot, the examination of it, the study of it – that is awareness shining light on subconscious, cognitive behaviors. Driving itself is not an instinct; it generally takes people a few attempts behind a wheel before someone is confident enough to drive on a highway. It requires a cognitive ability to adapt any stored memory (like how to drive a car) into completely new situations (even as simple of a new situation as a different combination of red and green lights on your daily work commute).

Analyzing those moments across time and situation is a powerful part of expospecture. Your entire life’s history is filled with a sample size of infinite amounts of data points. When your brain turned off in the driver’s seat, what were you thinking of? Was it the destination? Was it the vacation you’re saving up for? Maybe there was just a song on repeat stuck in your head, or maybe you were just tired and memorable thoughts took too long to form.

children.title: Do experiences prove identity even if they’re not remembered?

paragraphs.text: So if a human’s biological body died, but all of their memories were captured and immediately transferred to a clone at the moment of death, are they dead? If a person were to travel back in time to their exact moment ten years ago, without any memories or experience from those ten years, will anything be different? The Ship of Theseus paradox continues adding layers of complexity to conceptualizing identity. If awareness is forever lost upon bodily death, as in that your soul cannot be transferred from body to body, then how many transplants can a person get before they are no longer themselves? By the age of 80, the majority of cells in your body from birth have left and been replaced long ago.

Many people have been lucky and fortunate enough to have their heart replaced with another’s at a time where they would have otherwise died. Ancient Egyptians, Aristotle, Upanishads, and medieval Islamic and Christian philosophers argued cardiocentricism believing that the heart was essentially the command center for the psyche, or soul.,  If that’s the case, then is a person with a heart transplant the same person she was before the surgery? What about in the middle of the surgery during a heart-lung bypass when a machine takes the role of “animating the body”? Even in less dramatic situations, identity is being revised through puberty, trauma, migration, or just repeatedly hearing “you’re the smart one” or “you’re the troublemaker.”

I give more weight to the brain as being the source of the soul, but the logic applies. As technology and innovation increase at the rapid pace they have been, it would be foolish to assume that a brain transplant is impossible in the future. But until then, I have to ground myself in the technology of the day. Currently, Elon Musk and his team at Neuralink have already connected brain activity to technological devices. Trialists have begun to play video games without moving. Prosthetics are getting closer and closer to achieving full limb replacements by connecting signals to the brain. It’s not long before devices can regain hearing for a deaf person and restore some form of sight to a blind person.

By tweaking these senses, it is not simply providing sound or sight. This technology would channel a blind person’s brain to perceive their surroundings in a similar way to a sighted person. When you look at grass, your brain will perceive grass differently than a cow, which will perceive it differently than would another blade of grass. You might notice that it’s green or brown, tall or short, or something else. A cow might not know what it is aside from food. Humans are typically trichromats, while cows are dichromats, so the color of grass to them might not be much different than the color of a lake.

For us to look at a piece of grass and form these complex thoughts about it, these thoughts that don’t exist in a cow’s ability to comprehend, further proves the complexity of consciousness. A cow will look at grass and see “food” because it’s been programmed to for millennia and millennia. Archeologists specializing in the Cognitive Revolution of 75,000 years ago agree that consciousness, by our understanding, is unique to humans. We are so far the only collection of atoms with the ability to communicate and comprehend abstract ideas. Our brains are able to tap into that extra realm and choose to analyze the structure and qualities of the grass.

Endospection, then, is the metacognitive habit of internalizing and examining self-identity. I picture this work on the self as happening in and around a pulsing sphere of identity. I call that sphere the Endosphere: the current, always-changing configuration of who we take ourselves to be. Endospection names the habit of returning to, narrating, and revising that Endosphere over time. It is the disciplined practice of asking:
Who is the “I” doing this thinking?
How have my body, memories, technologies, and social labels helped build the story I call “myself”?
Which parts of that story feel given, and which have I chosen, or could I choose, to change?

In a school context, endospection is not an abstract thought experiment; it is the foundation for students monitoring their own learning, biases, and decisions. A curriculum that treats self-identity as fixed or invisible leaves that story to be written by accident: by algorithms, stereotypes, and whoever yells the loudest. A curriculum that centers endospection treats self-identity as the first object of study, giving students the tools to notice, question, and revise the narratives through which they think, learn, and act.

Students should not depend on curriculum evaluation tools or direction from others to decode the existence of a hidden curriculum. Because it is impossible to teach all of history, many high schools continually attempt to fit as much knowledge into lessons as possible. Still, some history teachers find themselves rushing to cram the last four decades of content into the final weeks of the year. The content-driven approach forces dependency on being told what to learn next, sacrificing the metacognitive habit of forming relationships between internal nodes of knowledge. Endospection pushes in the opposite direction: instead of training students to wait for the next unit, it trains them to notice and build connections among what they already know and who they already are.

Another limitation endospection resolves comes from a critical misunderstanding in content-first curriculum: it treats both history and identity as fixed facts to be delivered, rather than as stories that are constantly revised as the future unfolds. A curriculum that does not recognize that the future affects the past cannot easily accept individual growth and evolving identities. A core aspect of endospection is that both knowledge and identity are fluid and ever changing. Both on a societal and individual level, across two moments or two millennia, the values of individuals (which collectively form the values of society) fluctuate.

Less than five centuries ago, or around twenty generations ago, geocentrism was the dominant belief; the reality for sixteenth-century peasants and emperors, farmers and kings, was simply that the earth was the center of existence. Without a comprehension of the universe, gravity, rotation, or astrophysics, that was reality. History curriculum is rewritten every generation; as historiography changes, different interpretations of historical realities shed new light on entire foundations. Endospective practice makes this explicit for students: what feels like “reality” in one moment may later be understood as one interpretation among many.

How will future generations view us? Will our reality of current events be similar to the reality taught in classrooms two hundred years from now? Will our reality of current events be similar to our own recollection of this time ten years from now? Without a persistent photographic memory, and without being able to recreate the exact conditions under which an event happened, all that is left is the concept or takeaway. Even with written, photographic, or video evidence, the recreation of the moment becomes limited by one’s current endospection; we do not return to the event itself, but to the event as refracted through who we have become.

For teachers, endospection means designing tasks that explicitly ask students to revisit their own prior thinking, compare it to their present perspective, and name what changed and why. For students, it means developing the habit of noticing how new experiences, new information, and new futures reshape the stories they tell about themselves and their world – rather than assuming that “who I am” and “what really happened” were settled long ago.

Intentional control and ownership over one’s reality is a product of a metacognitive curriculum. This control and ownership is forged through practice, preparation, and prediction. While it is not necessary to carve out special time for endospection (endospection is possible in every moment) intentional and productive awareness of it should be offered to students in the form of structured opportunities.

Endospection is not simply answering direct questions such as “What are my values?” or “What are my thoughts regarding my political identity?” While there are aspects of metacognition embedded in these questions, they remain cognitively surface-level; the emphasis is on the what. Endospection invites further exploration into the why and how. More important questions become “How do I incorporate my values in my daily life?” or “Why do I value honesty?”

Other opportunities to engage in metacognitive endologue can be more indirect. A class project might encourage students to design an autobiography where the medium itself reflects their sense of self. This added dimension not only allows for differentiated journeys and outcomes; it also directs endospection as students decide how to represent their lives. One student who is musically gifted might compose a four-part arrangement, transposing the key or tempo to mimic different parts of their life. Another student might code a digital scrapbook with animation, designing the horizontal and vertical flow along axes of their values.

There is no floor to the depth of exploration of self-identity. With each new experience, one’s understanding of reality is altered. Without the opportunity to explore how new ideas affect old ideas, students are left in a confused state, hoping that their recall and memorization abilities will get them an A. Not only does our understanding of knowledge change, but so do our values. Even the foundations from which those values emerge reconstruct over time. Opportunities for students to continue exploring their own identity through metacognitive endospection are effectively endless.
Endospecture is the habit of disciplined self-inquiry that utilizes the awareness of internal unknowability to build a sovereign foundation for all external understanding

AMC Studios released a two-season show called Pantheon in 2022 on the topic of Uploaded Intelligence. Although it’s set in a near-future version of our world, the technology it depicts is far beyond what we can currently do; the ethical questions it raises, however, are squarely aimed at our present moment. In Pantheon, advances in artificial intelligence and neurotechnology allow private corporations to scan a person’s brain, encode their memories, sensations, and personality onto hard drives, and in the process destroy their biological body. Can the self be preserved in an artificial environment without the biological components such as the brain, heart, or perhaps a separate soul?

Debates with friends and family over specific episodes showed me the range of perspectives. The conclusion I came to does not imply “correctness,” simply a justified conclusion: as long as the self is believed in, the self exists. Much like the concepts of race, sexuality, currency, or social status, the conception of the self is based on experience-formed awareness conducted by memory. There is a sense in which the self is a story we continuously tell and retell.

At the same time, self-identity, as determined by René Descartes, is the only truth beyond doubt. In his Meditations, Descartes found this kind of radical self-examination to be difficult, even frightening. When he tried to doubt the reality of everything, he brushed up against nihilism before finding an anchor in simple logic. Doubting, he realized, requires thinking; doubting that you are thinking is itself a form of thought. If thought makes doubting possible, and doubting is already a kind of thinking, then the existence of a thinking self cannot be doubted out of existence. For Descartes, the self does not depend on what you believe about the world; it is guaranteed by the very act of thinking, the cogito – I think, therefore I am.

From a contemporary perspective, this raises an uncomfortable question: when, if ever, does that thinking self actually “switch off”? Everyday life already offers liminal cases. During deep, dreamless sleep, people report no conscious experience at all, even though brain activity continues and dreaming can occur in other sleep stages. Neuroscience studies show that consciousness during sleep waxes and wanes with changes in large-scale brain activity, particularly in posterior cortical regions that support the content of experience.

General anesthesia provides an even sharper edge. Rather than shutting the brain down, anesthetic drugs reversibly alter consciousness by disrupting the functional connectivity of cortical networks (especially frontoparietal and thalamocortical circuits) so that integrated, reportable experience temporarily disappears even as neural activity continues. Patients typically “wake up” with no memory of the interval, yet we assume the same person went under and came back.

In a less medical simplification: at these edges of deep sleep (anesthesia, and, more finally, death the continuity of the self breaks. Biological processes and neural activity may persist or resume. But from the first-person point of view there are gaps in experience that force us to ask whether an unbroken, thinking self is something that exists in fact or something we continuously reconstruct from memory once awareness returns. For a metacognitive curriculum, this matters: students are not just “having” experiences; they are constantly stitching them into a story of who they are.
But where do those experiences come from?

children.title: Curriculum Fences and the Role of Structure

paragraphs.text: Content-specific structure is not inherently “bad.” Courses, schedules, and syllabi exist for reasons that are not purely oppressive. They can protect students from chaos, ensure access to foundational knowledge, and make shared discourse possible. What becomes corrosive is when content structure is treated as the foundation of education rather than as scaffolding built around deeper habits like omnipere and endospection.

Even though omnipere operates on a more abstract, conceptual dimension than cognitive exploration within a single subject, it does not float above content. It uses content as raw material. Omniperegrination moves through art, physics, welding, literature, history, and every other subject or field. That is why this book does not discard subjects or communication; there are five other habits and a three-dimensional compass (explained later) that attend to structure, assessment, and socially accepted “truths.” Omnipere’s distinct contribution is to break from the assumption that structure is the starting point, and instead position structure as one possible anchor for curiosity.

children.title: Omnipere in Practice: From Welding to Worlds

paragraphs.text: Omniperegrination can be as narrow or as wide as a student’s intentional curiosity allows. It can remain strictly within a discipline or stretch across many. The key variable is not the breadth of the journey but the learner’s stance toward it.
Take welding. At first glance, it appears purely technical: amperage, heat, bond strength, metallurgy, safety protocols. But welding can become a grounding point for omniperegrination:
A student might begin by wondering why certain metals fuse more easily than others, leading to questions about atomic structure and chemical bonding.

From there, the concepts of joining, tension, fracture, and solidifying may begin to operate as metaphors: how do relationships hold or break, how do communities fuse or split, how do ideas become “fixed” or remain malleable?
Soldering two wires together to form a new circuit becomes an image for creating partnerships, writing policy that binds groups, or composing music that welds discordant themes into a coherent whole.

At that point, the omniperegrination has moved from strictly technical understanding to abstract and fluid meaning-making. The act of welding is still itself, there is no requirement to turn shop class into a philosophy seminar. But it has become a node connected to a much wider network of ideas. The student has not necessarily “answered” a defined research question, yet their capacity to think with and through welding has expanded.
In this sense, omnipere does not require schools to abandon practical, content-specific learning. It invites teachers to treat each domain as a launchpad rather than a cage.

children.title: Autonomy, Power, and the Expansion of Exospection

paragraphs.text: The goal of this (and the other) habit(s) is to prevent one’s reality from being silently suppressed or flattened by dominant narratives, individual biases, or narrow definitions of what counts as legitimate thinking. Omnipere works by building relationships between past and new nodes of thought, ideas, beliefs, perceptions, curiosities, and events (both autobiographical and external). It is a form of autonomous thought: opportunities can be provided by teachers, institutions, or peers; guidance and structure can be present; collaboration can shape the journey. But the actual omniperegrination happens within the learner’s own cognitive landscape and is as fluid as endospection.

A student who has had repeated opportunities to omniperegrinate develops a reality with more internal room. That expanded internal reality directly strengthens what I later call exospection: the habit of understanding and acting within the realities of other. When learners are practiced at noticing and re-routing their own thinking, following threads across domains, and integrating new perspectives into their graph of meaning, they are better equipped to recognize that other people’s realities are likewise complex, layered, and in motion. In that sense, omnipere is not a luxury add-on to a content curriculum. It is one of the most effective ways to expand exospection and, by extension, to support democratic, anti-oppressive education.

Endospection and Omnipere together define the inner landscape of metacognition in this model: who I am, and how my thinking is allowed to travel. The remaining habits take that inner mobility and connect it to evidence, evaluation, other people’s realities, and public action. By legitimizing intentional exploration as a core metacognitive habit, schools can help students resist being trapped inside a single, imposed way of understanding the world and instead cultivate the capacity to move through many.

Up to this point, I have been describing the first two habits of a metacognitive curriculum through a pulsing sphere of selfhood and particles of controlled wander. I call that sphere the Endosphere: the current, always-changing configuration of who we take ourselves to be. Endospection names the work we do on that Endosphere – the ongoing habit of revisiting our own story, testing and revising the meanings we give to our experiences, and noticing how our sense of “who I am” shifts over time.

From the surface of the Endosphere, small units of meaning are constantly being produced. Whenever an experience stands out like a sharp comment, a memorable line, a solved equation, or a disturbing headline, a part of it becomes a discrete unit we can, in principle, return to. I call these units noema. A noema can be as simple as “2 + 2 = 4,” as complex as “the summer I almost drowned,” or as general as “people with power usually cannot be trusted.” What matters for this curriculum is that a noema can separate from the Endosphere, move, combine with other noema, and later be recalled, reinterpreted, or let go.

Omnipere and its unfolding, omniperegrination, describe a particular stance toward these noema. Instead of fixing them into conclusions right away, the learner allows them to move. Noema emerge from the Endosphere and drift in cognitive space. Some stay close, others move farther away. They bump into each other, sometimes form loose clusters, and sometimes drift apart again. Over time, some clusters become denser and start to pull in additional noema. From the learner’s point of view, these denser regions feel like recurring themes or hunches: experiences around fairness and discipline at school, an ongoing interest in maps, a persistent worry about climate, or a repeated curiosity about why certain rules in math always seem to work. Omnipere does not require that these patterns be named or finalized. It simply ensures that the wandering is intentional and that noema are given a chance to connect.

However, wandering alone does not answer the question of what to do with these patterns. At some point, a learner has to decide which clusters of noema are worth deeper attention and how to follow them up. Not every cluster needs the same level of focus. This is where the next habit enters: Constellare.
Omnipere is the freeing habit of intentional, self-driven wandering to reclaim the autonomy of inquiry and expand the internal landscape of meaning.

At some point in their schooling, students inevitably endologue questions such as, “Why do I have to learn this?” or “When will I ever use this?” The unfortunate presumptive reality regarding the perception of schools incites student trepidation. When correctness is treated as pre-determined and the curriculum is framed as something already justified, students learn, often unconsciously, to subordinate their curiosity to institutional expectations.

Omnipere emerges as the antidote: a metacognitive habit that legitimizes wandering, wondering, and intellectual movement without predetermined destinations. It is the practice of allowing thought to travel across disciplines, experiences, identities, and imagined possibilities without first asking whether such travel is required or assessable. In a system that too often trains learners to wait for permission before thinking broadly, omnipere restores the birthright of exploration, treating curiosity not as a distraction from learning but as one of its highest forms.

Omniperegrination names the journey that follows when this habit is activated: the unfolding, recursive movement by which a learner follows a thread of interest wherever it leads, weaving new connections into their evolving reality.

Emphasis on exploration and curiosity is certainly not new in philosophy or education. Omnipere crystallizes several strands of curriculum thought that have long gestured toward exploration but rarely named it as a distinct metacognitive habit.

Dewey’s experimental education positioned experience and inquiry at the heart of schooling. In his cycle of impulse, curiosity, problem, and reflection, genuine learning begins when a puzzling situation interrupts the flow of routine and the learner feels compelled to “try something out.” Exploration, in Deweyan terms, is not ornamental; it is the starting point for thinking. Yet even in Dewey’s most generous formulations, the school day is still structured around teacher-defined problems and subjects. Students may experiment within a frame, but the frame itself is usually not up for renegotiation.

Reconceptualist theorists, especially Pinar, pushed exploration into autobiographical terrain through currere, where the learner revisits past events, imagines possible futures, and interrogates the present to re-narrate their educational life. This is a form of exploration, but it is primarily temporal and reflective while leaning heavily on what I have called endospection: examining how the self has been constructed over time.

More recent student-led and recursive models attempt to place exploration at the center of classroom structure itself. In these designs, students co-create units, generate driving questions, and sometimes even set the sequence of study. The class “recurses” on its own work, using each project as the seed for the next. At the extreme, the teacher becomes facilitator of a curriculum that is almost entirely emergent from student interests.

Omnipere sits in conversation with all three currents but diverges in important ways. With Dewey, it shares the conviction that curiosity is a starting condition of meaningful learning. With currere, it shares an emphasis on identity and autobiographical meaning-making. With student-led designs, it shares a commitment to honoring student questions as legitimate drivers of curricular movement.

But omnipere is one habit among six, not a totalizing model of schooling. It does not ask teachers to abandon structure, nor does it assume that the only “authentic” learning is fully student-run. Instead, it treats exploration as a metacognitive stance that can live inside structured environments and alongside other habits. Where fully emergent approaches sometimes collapse under the weight of boundless choice, omnipere is deliberately bounded: it guarantees the right to wander, but not the obligation to wander all the time.
Because omnipere is the freest of the habits, it is easy to mistake it for things it is not:

First, omnipere is not mere distraction or passive daydreaming. A student staring out the window and mentally replaying last night’s argument may be thinking vividly, but unless a spark of curiosity appears (eg: “How did we get there? Could that have gone differently? What does this say about how I handle conflict?”), the experience has not yet become omniperegrination. Omnipere presumes intentional curiosity: a felt pull to follow a question, pattern, or phenomenon beyond its original frame. A student who cannot control their thoughts, or explore curiosities intentionally, does not omniperegrinate; they only drift.

Second, omnipere is not yet research. Research, as I define it later, is curiosity that has been harnessed toward a goal: it involves framing questions, selecting methods, gathering evidence, and iterating toward some provisional answer or product. Omnipere precedes this, but in no way is “less important” or “easier.” It is the open-ended phase in which the learner allows questions to multiply without demanding that they immediately become answerable or useful. To omniperegrinate is to explore without knowing in advance which inquiries will crystallize into research problems.

Third, omnipere is not the same as critical reflection. Critical thinking and reflection can and should attend to omniperegrinations; they evaluate sources, identify biases, and ask how new ideas fit into or disrupt one’s reality. But omnipere itself does not require closure. One can omniperegrinate without ever arriving at a tidy “why.” The learning happens in the expansion and reconfiguration of the internal knowledge graph: new nodes, new edges, new possible paths between what once seemed unrelated.

For this reason, it is unhelpful to speak of “productive” versus “unproductive” omnipere. Omnipere, by definition, is productive: the moment exploration becomes intentional, it is already restructuring the learner’s reality, even if no assignment is finished and no conclusion is written down. The more meaningful contrast is between omniperegrination and its counterfeits: algorithmic wandering, compliant busywork disguised as choice, or “student voice” narrowed to pre-approved options.

Consider a student in an art class who notices that two pigments, when blended, create a surprising shade. Omnipere begins with a simple, honest question: Why does that color look like that? From there, omniperegrination might unfold along a chain like this:
The student wonders how light interacts with pigment, and begins reading or watching videos about wavelengths, absorption, and reflection.

This leads to curiosity about how different creatures perceive color: humans as trichromats, some animals as dichromats or tetrachromats. “Color” is no longer just paint on a canvas but a biologically contingent, species-specific phenomenon.
From there, the student begins thinking about other invisible structures like sound waves, radio signals, Wi-Fi, cosmic radiation. What else exists in the room that cannot be seen?
That, in turn, raises questions about invisible realities in religion or philosophy: spirits, forces, energies, karma. How do cultures name and interpret what cannot be directly perceived?
This curiosity then drifts toward dimensionality: how might a two-dimensional being understand a three-dimensional world, and what does that metaphor suggest about the limits of human perception?
The student finds resources on string theory’s higher dimensions and starts connecting 2D art, 3D space, and speculative multidimensional models.

The initial “why does this color appear this way?” may never be fully resolved in a formal sense. At any point, any of those questions could have splintered off into any other question. Yet during the omnipere, the student has:
encountered new conceptual tools (wavelength, spectrum, perception),
developed new metaphors for invisible structure, and
connected art to physics, philosophy, and cosmology.

Their internal reality has shifted; the network of concepts through which they understand the world is more complex and more flexible. That is omniperegrination: not a straight line from question to answer, but an intentional wandering through adjacent possibilities.

In classic public schooling, the ability to omniperegrinate like this is often limited to the content within the course. In a typical middle school art class, the syllabus will not include objectives around sound waves, religious metaphors, or higher dimensions. The links between 2D geometric constructions in math, 2D composition in art, and higher-dimensional models in physics rarely surface. Omnipere names the habit that notices those possible connections and begins walking them anyway.

children.title: Constellare: Research, Purposeful Organization of Noema

paragraphs.text: For curriculum design, Constellare raises a different set of questions than Endospection and Omnipere. If Endospection asks, “How does this unit give students tools to examine who they are?” and Omnipere asks, “Where in this unit are students allowed to wander and connect ideas on their own terms?”, Constellare asks: “Where, when, and how does this unit support students in turning wandering into research?” A metacognitive curriculum cannot assume that this transition will happen automatically. It must build in structures where students are prompted to choose a cluster of noema, frame a “so what?” question, and organize evidence or experiences around that question in a deliberate way.

In a conventional content-first design, it is easy to tuck Constellare back inside familiar boxes: “research in history,” “inquiry in science,” “projects in welding.” That is not the architecture I am proposing. In a metacognitive curriculum (or contexture), the primary unit of design is not the subject but the opportunity. A structured opening for students to exercise habits like Endospection, Omnipere, and Constellare with sufficient depth and support. Content still matters, but curriculum should incorporate it not because it belongs to “ninth-grade history,” but because it offers rich noema to constellate.

From this perspective, Constellare does not live inside history or science classes; those categories are secondary, if they appear at all. Instead, a term or year is built from a sequence of interdisciplinary opportunities, each framed around a theme or problem that invites students to turn clusters of noema into constellations. Knowledge from history, science, literature, or technical fields enter as sources of noema (cases, data, stories, tools) that students draw on as needed for their constellaration.
You can imagine a few types of opportunities (or contextures) that make this concrete:

Opportunity: Evidence and Power.Students begin by omniperegrinating through examples of how decisions get justified in different arenas: court cases, school discipline policies, public health campaigns, family rules, religious teachings, scientific debates. These are not “units” from different subjects; they are all sources of noema around the same theme.
