notes.text: Most mainstream frameworks gesture at refraction-adjacent work but stop short of the move that makes it refraction. They produce content about how lenses work without producing the practice of watching your own lens work in real time. The distinction is subtle but consequential.Let me go framework by framework.Critical Race Theory (academic, not the K-12 boogeyman version)CRT in its actual scholarly form (Bell, Crenshaw, Delgado, Matsuda) is doing something close to refraction, but at a structural rather than individual level. It examines how legal and social systems carry racial assumptions that shape what counts as neutral, fair, or natural. The "interest convergence" thesis, intersectionality, the critique of colorblindness, all of these are lens-noticing moves. They reveal how the apparatus of law and policy bends what gets seen as racism.Where it falls short of refraction: CRT trains students to notice the system's lens, not their own. A student fluent in CRT can articulate how American law has structurally privileged whiteness without ever asking how their own analytical patterns, their reading habits, their first-source-trust, their tone-before-evidence weighting, are bent by the lens they carry. CRT gives the student a powerful new lens and asks them to look through it. Refraction would ask them to examine that new lens with the same rigor they applied to the old one.This is not a critique of CRT's scholarly project. It's a description of what CRT was designed to do (structural analysis) versus what refraction does (apparatus analysis at the individual level). They're complementary, not competing.Culturally Responsive Pedagogy (Ladson-Billings, Gay, Hammond)CRP is closer to refraction than CRT in some ways and further in others. Closer because it explicitly invites students to bring their cultural lenses into the classroom and treats those lenses as legitimate epistemological positions, not deficits. Hammond's Culturally Responsive Teaching and the Brain in particular pushes toward something like refractal awareness in students.Further because CRP's primary audience is teachers, not students. The lens-noticing CRP does best is the teacher noticing their own lens (which is genuinely refractive work for the teacher). For students, CRP often validates rather than examines. A student's cultural ways of knowing are affirmed as legitimate, which is right and necessary, but the next move (now examine how that cultural lens bends what you see, in this moment, with this material) is rarely taken. Refraction would take it.Where CRP overlaps with refraction is in its emphasis on what Hammond calls "cognitive routines." That's lens-knowledge in everything but name. But CRP doesn't typically scaffold the practice of catching one's own routine in the act, which is what makes it refraction rather than self-affirmation.Anti-racist pedagogy (Kendi, DiAngelo, Tatum, Singleton's Courageous Conversations)This is where the gap is widest. Anti-racist pedagogy in most popular forms (especially DiAngelo and Kendi as adopted in K-12 PD) supplies a predetermined lens and asks students or teachers to refract their thinking through it. The lens is given; the work is applying it.This is exactly the move we discussed earlier with critical pedagogy. The pedagogy substitutes one lens for another and rarely teaches students to examine the new lens with the same rigor they were taught to examine the old one. A student who has internalized DiAngelo's framework will catch white fragility in real time but may not catch their own framework's bending of how they read every interracial interaction. The practice of noticing the apparatus has been replaced by the practice of applying the apparatus.Singleton's Courageous Conversations protocol is partial exception. Its "Four Agreements" (stay engaged, speak your truth, experience discomfort, expect and accept non-closure) are scaffolding for something that could become refraction if extended. But the protocol's primary aim is racial dialogue, not lens-examination, and refraction is incidental to that aim rather than the point.XQ Redesign and similar reform initiativesXQ, Big Picture Learning, NewSchools, High Tech High, and most of the "redesign" ecosystem are doing something different again. Their frameworks emphasize student agency, project-based learning, real-world relevance, and competency-based assessment. These are valuable moves. They are not refraction.XQ's published "Learner Outcomes" include things like "thoughtful learners" and "original thinkers" and "broadly literate." These are content categories or dispositions. None of them name the practice of examining one's own apparatus. The closest gesture is usually toward "metacognition" as a generic competency, which the rubrics treat as awareness-of-strategy ("I know I learn better by writing") rather than awareness-of-apparatus ("I know my analytical pattern privileges first impressions and I can watch that pattern operate in real time").The XQ framework is also content-organized, not habit-organized. It assumes students will encounter content (history, science, etc.) and develop competencies through that encounter. Your framework inverts this. The habits are the foundation; content is the material the habits practice on. XQ doesn't make this inversion.The pattern across all of themMainstream frameworks tend to do one of three things, none of which is refraction:Substitute lenses. Replace an unexamined dominant lens with an examined-but-now-prescribed alternative lens. Anti-racist pedagogy in its popular forms; some critical pedagogy.Validate lenses. Affirm the legitimacy of students' existing lenses without asking them to examine those lenses' operation. Some CRP applications.Bypass lenses. Focus on skills, competencies, agency, or projects without making lens-examination central. XQ and most redesign initiatives.Refraction does none of these. It teaches the student to notice that a lens is operating, examine its settings, watch it bend the current encounter, and adjust where adjustment serves the inquiry. The lens being examined can be anything: nationalism, anti-nationalism, CRT-derived analysis, CRP-affirmed cultural identity, the content of a religious upbringing, the framework of the teacher in the room. Refraction is prior to the choice of lens. It is the capacity that lets the student engage any lens, including the one being handed to them, with their eyes open.Where the closest fits actually liveIf you want to cite frameworks that are doing genuinely refraction-adjacent work, the strongest candidates aren't in mainstream curriculum design at all. They're in:Conceptual change theory (Posner, Strike, Hewson, Gertzog 1982; Vosniadou's later work). This literature studies how learners revise existing conceptions when confronted with anomalies, which is structurally close to what refractals do. It's mostly in science education research.Threshold concepts (Meyer and Land 2003). The idea that some concepts are "troublesome knowledge" that requires the learner to undergo a transformation of perspective to grasp. The transformation itself is described in terms close to refraction.Reflective practice (Schön's The Reflective Practitioner, 1983). Schön's "reflection-in-action" is the closest mainstream concept to refraction: the practitioner watching themselves practice, in the moment, and adjusting. Schön is talking about professionals (architects, therapists, etc.) rather than students, but the cognitive move is essentially refractive.Phenomenography (Marton, in Swedish education research). Studies how learners experience phenomena differently and treats those differences as the object of pedagogical attention. Close to refraction in spirit.Mezirow's transformative learning (1991, 2000). His "disorienting dilemma" and "critical reflection on assumptions" are reaching for something refraction-like, though Mezirow's framework is goal-directed in a way refraction isn't.If your dissertation needs scholarly anchors for refraction, those five literatures are where to dig. None of them is a complete fit; each does part of the work. Your contribution is naming the habit precisely, distinguishing it from neighboring habits in a coherent system, and giving it a curricular structure (the Contexture) rather than leaving it as a description of what some learners happen to do.The honest claim for your dissertation is something like: refraction names a metacognitive habit that several scholarly traditions have approached from different angles without integrating. Conceptual change theory studies what refraction produces. Reflective practice studies refraction in professional contexts. CRP gestures at refraction in teachers. CRT works at the structural level. None of them treat refraction as a teachable, scaffolded habit with a curricular home. This framework does.That's a defensible original contribution and one that doesn't require you to dismiss the existing literature. It positions your work as integrative and operational, which is honest about what you're actually doing.
